docs.title: methods.lock Format
docs.text:
The methods.lock file records, for every remote dependency of a package, the exact resolved version, the tree digest of what was fetched, the semantic fingerprint of what it means, and the provenance of where it came from. It is auto-generated and SHOULD be committed to version control.

Implementation status

The lock file is committed design. This section is the contract implementations are brought into conformance with — the same forward-contract convention the Library Crate Format uses for its unrealized sections. Conformance is asserted against this document as each piece lands.

docs.title: A Verification Record, Not a Resolution Record
docs.text: Because version resolution is Minimum Version Selection, the build list is fully determined by the manifests and the published version tags — no resolution-time state and no registry oracle enters it: the lock file can be regenerated at any time from the manifests plus the fetched sources, and regeneration reproduces the same entries as long as the repositories' published version tags — which tags exist, and which commits they point at — have not changed. The lock is therefore a verification record — it exists so that a later install can prove it fetched the same bytes and the same meaning the original resolution saw — not a resolution record that a resolver consults to decide versions. This is the same relationship go.sum has to go.mod.

docs.title: File Name and Location
docs.text: The lock file MUST be named methods.lock and MUST be located at the root of the package directory, alongside METHODS.toml.

docs.title: File Encoding and Syntax
docs.text: methods.lock MUST be a valid TOML document encoded in UTF-8.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The lock file is a flat TOML document where each top-level table key is a package address, and the value is a table containing the locked metadata for that package.

["github.com/mthds/document-processing"]
version     = "1.2.3"
digest      = "sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2"
fingerprint = "7c9e2b4f8a1d3e5c7b9f2a4d6e8c1b3f5a7d9e2c4b6f8a1d3e5c7b9f2a4d6e8c"
source      = "https://github.com/mthds/document-processing.git"
commit      = "8f5b2c1a9d3e7f4b6a8c2e5d1f9b3a7c4e6d8f2b"

["github.com/mthds/scoring-lib"]
version     = "0.5.1"
digest      = "sha256:e5f6a7b8c9d0e5f6a7b8c9d0e5f6a7b8c9d0e5f6a7b8c9d0e5f6a7b8c9d0e5f6"
fingerprint = "2d4f6a8c1e3b5d7f9a2c4e6b8d1f3a5c7e9b2d4f6a8c1e3b5d7f9a2c4e6b8d1f"
source      = "https://github.com/mthds/scoring-lib.git"
commit      = "3a7c4e6d8f2b8f5b2c1a9d3e7f4b6a8c2e5d1f9b"

Because package addresses contain dots and slashes, they MUST be quoted as TOML keys.

docs.title: Locked Package Fields
docs.text:
Each entry in the lock file contains:

Field Type Required Description version string Yes The exact resolved version. MUST be valid semver. digest string Yes The tree digest of the fetched package's tree. MUST match the pattern sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}. Records what was fetched. fingerprint string Yes The semantic fingerprint of the dependency's resolved content — the library crate fingerprint of the library the dependency's package resolves into, as a 64-character lowercase hex digest. Records what it means. source string Yes The HTTPS clone URL the package was fetched from, derived from the address (see Fetching Remote Dependencies). MUST start with https:// and MUST end with .git. commit string Yes The commit SHA the resolved version tag pointed to at lock time, as a 40-character lowercase hex digest. Provenance: a tag can be re-pointed; the commit cannot. It is also the honest cache key for tooling that caches clones.

The digest and the fingerprint are two deliberately distinct digests joined per dependency at this one point. The tree digest is transport integrity: it changes when any fetched byte changes, including formatting and comments. The fingerprint is semantic identity: it is stable across reformatting and changes exactly when the dependency's effective type surface, prompts, or entry points change. Together they let tooling verify a fetch and explain an update — a version bump whose fingerprint is unchanged changed nothing a consumer can observe; one whose fingerprint moved can be diffed semantically.

docs.title: Digest Computation
docs.text: The digest is the tree digest of the dependency's package tree: the SHA-256 of the tree's listing, one sha256sum line per file sorted by tree path byte for byte, written sha256: followed by the 64-character lowercase hex digest. The tree is the one Method Tree: Dependencies Are Trees of Their Own defines for a fetched package: the files of the package's directory in the resolved commit, read from the commit's git objects as stored and filtered by the membership rule with that commit's own .gitignore files. Anyone can recompute it from the commit with coreutils and git alone.

docs.title: Locks Written Before Tree Digests
docs.text: A lock written before standard 7.0.0 records a hash field in each entry, computed by an algorithm that concatenated paths and file contents with no separator, so two different directories could share one hash. A compliant implementation MUST refuse, when it parses the lock, any entry carrying a hash field, with a message saying that the lock predates tree digests and that running lock regenerates it. It MUST NOT verify a hash, so an untouched dependency of an old lock is never reported as tampered with. Since the lock is a regenerable verification record, regenerating it is always safe.

docs.title: Fingerprint Computation
docs.text: The fingerprint is the library crate fingerprint of the dependency's resolved content: the dependency package is resolved into a library on its own (its bundles as the host, its own dependencies folded in per that specification), normalized, and fingerprinted per the crate specification's canonicalization rules. It is recomputable by any consumer from the fetched source — no registry or third party has to be trusted to have computed it honestly.

docs.title: Which Packages Are Locked
docs.text:
• Remote dependencies (those without a path field in the root manifest) are locked, including all transitive remote dependencies.
  • Local path dependencies are NOT locked. They are resolved from the filesystem at load time and are expected to change during development.

docs.title: When the Lock File Updates
docs.text:
The lock file is regenerated when the manifests change or when a tool re-locks:

  • lock — resolves all dependencies from the manifests and writes the lock file. Because resolution is deterministic, re-running lock against unchanged manifests and unchanged published version tags — the same tags, pointing at the same commits — reproduces the same file.
  • add — records the added dependency's latest version as its floor in METHODS.toml, then re-locks.
  • update — raises the floors in METHODS.toml to the latest available versions, then re-locks. Under MVS, re-resolution alone never moves a version: updating is a deliberate manifest edit, and the re-lock records its result. See Version Resolution Strategy.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
When installing from a lock file, a compliant implementation MUST:

  1. For each entry in the lock file, locate the corresponding fetched or cached package directory.
  2. Recompute the tree digest of that package's tree, as described above, either from the files of the cached copy as written, every file at its path, without applying the membership rule again, or from the commit, filtered by the membership rule as Dependencies Are Trees of Their Own states.
  3. Compare the computed digest with the digest field in the lock file.
  4. Reject the installation if any digest does not match (integrity failure). A mismatch is a hard failure, never a warning.

An implementation SHOULD additionally recompute the fingerprint and report a mismatch: a tree digest that matches while the fingerprint does not indicates a defect in one of the implementations, since the fingerprint is a pure function of the fetched content.

docs.title: Deterministic Output
docs.text:
Lock file entries MUST be sorted by package address (lexicographic ascending) to produce deterministic output suitable for clean version control diffs.

An empty lock file (no remote dependencies) MAY be an empty file or absent entirely.

Copy Markdown

docs.title: METHODS.toml Manifest Format
docs.text: The METHODS.toml file is the package manifest — the identity card and dependency declaration for an MTHDS package. It MUST be named exactly METHODS.toml and MUST be located at the root of the package directory.

docs.title: File Encoding and Syntax
docs.text: METHODS.toml MUST be a valid TOML document encoded in UTF-8.

docs.title: Top-Level Sections
docs.text:
A METHODS.toml file contains up to three top-level sections:

Section Required Description [package] Yes Package identity and metadata. [dependencies] No Dependencies on other MTHDS packages. [exports] No Visibility declarations for pipes.

docs.title: The [package] Section
docs.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes The name of the method. MUST be snake_case (matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]*), 2-25 characters. See Name. address string Yes Globally unique package identifier. MUST follow the hostname/path pattern. display_name string No Human-friendly display label. When provided, MUST NOT be empty or whitespace-only, MUST NOT exceed 128 characters, and MUST NOT contain Unicode control characters (category Cc). Leading and trailing whitespace is stripped. version string Yes Package version. MUST be valid semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, with optional pre-release and build metadata). description string Yes Human-readable summary of the package's purpose. MUST NOT be empty. authors array of strings No List of author identifiers (e.g., "Name <email>"). Default: empty list. license string No SPDX license identifier (e.g., "MIT", "Apache-2.0"). mthds_version string No MTHDS standard version constraint. If set, MUST be a valid version constraint. main_pipe string No The package's entry-point pipe code. MUST be snake_case (matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]*). Auto-exported by virtue of being main_pipe. See Main Pipe. exclude array of strings No Patterns, in .gitignore syntax, naming files to keep out of the package's method tree. See Exclude.

docs.title: Address Format
docs.text:
The package address is the globally unique identifier for the package. It doubles as the fetch location for VCS-based distribution.

For a package at its repository root, the manifest address alone is that identity. In a library repository — a repository hosting several packages — the packages share the repository's address in their manifests, and each package's full, globally unique address is address + "/" + name (see Name and Distribution: Locating a Package Inside a Clone).

Pattern: ^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+\.[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+/[a-zA-Z0-9._/-]+$

In plain language: the address MUST start with a hostname (containing at least one dot), followed by a /, followed by one or more path segments.

Examples of valid addresses:

github.com/acme/legal-tools
github.com/mthds/document-processing
gitlab.com/company/internal-methods

Examples of invalid addresses:

legal-tools                     # No hostname
acme/legal-tools                # No dot in hostname

docs.title: Name
docs.text:
The name field is the name of the method. It is the primary identifier for the method — it appears in CLI output, registry listings, and documentation.

Constraints:

  • MUST be snake_case, matching the pattern [a-z][a-z0-9_]*.
  • MUST be between 2 and 25 characters.
  • MUST NOT be empty.

The manifest is the identity: the directory (or repository) that contains a package may carry any name, and a compliant tool MUST NOT require the directory name to match name. Where a fetched or cached copy of a package lives on disk is a tool concern, not part of the standard.

The name also participates in locating a package inside a repository that hosts several packages: a package's full address is its address when the package sits at the repository root, or address + "/" + name when it is one of several packages in a library repository. See Distribution: Locating a Package Inside a Clone.

Example:

[package]
name    = "nda_analyzer"
address = "github.com/acme/legal-tools"

docs.title: Display Name
docs.text:
The optional display_name field provides a human-friendly label for the package. It appears in CLI output, registry listings, and error messages. It is cosmetic only — the address remains the sole canonical identifier.

Constraints:

  • MUST NOT be empty or whitespace-only when provided.
  • MUST NOT exceed 128 characters (after leading/trailing whitespace is stripped).
  • MUST NOT contain Unicode control characters (Unicode general category Cc).
  • Emojis and other Unicode characters are allowed.
  • Leading and trailing whitespace is stripped by a compliant implementation.

Example:

[package]
name         = "nda_analyzer"
address      = "github.com/acme/legal-tools"
display_name = "Nda Analyzer"

docs.title: Version Format
docs.text:
The version field MUST conform to Semantic Versioning 2.0.0:

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-pre-release][+build-metadata]

Examples: 1.0.0, 0.3.0, 2.1.3-beta.1, 1.0.0-rc.1+build.42

docs.title: mthds_version Constraints
docs.text:
The mthds_version field, if present, declares which versions of the MTHDS standard this package is compatible with. It uses version constraint syntax (see Version Constraint Syntax).

The current MTHDS standard version is 8.0.0. See Versioning for what moves it.

docs.title: Main Pipe
docs.text:
The optional main_pipe field designates the package's primary entry point — the pipe that runs when a user invokes the package by name or address:

mthds run method nda_analyzer
mthds run method github.com/acme/legal-tools

Constraints:

  • The value MUST be a valid snake_case pipe code (matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]*).
  • The referenced pipe is auto-exported: it is part of the package's public surface by virtue of being main_pipe, whether or not it also appears in [exports]. There is no requirement to list it there. See The [exports] Section.
  • When main_pipe is not set, the package has no default entry point. It can still be consumed as a library by importing specific pipes.

Example:

[package]
name      = "nda_analyzer"
address   = "github.com/acme/legal-tools"
version   = "0.3.0"
main_pipe = "analyze_nda"

docs.title: Exclude
docs.text:
The optional exclude field lists patterns naming files to keep out of the package's method tree without keeping them out of git, such as sample data an author keeps in the repository but that no run needs:

[package]
name    = "invoice_letters"
address = "github.com/acme/invoice-letters"
version = "1.0.0"
exclude = ["samples/", "*.psd"]

Constraints:

  • Each entry is one pattern in the syntax of a .gitignore file, as gitignore documents it, and MUST NOT hold a line break. An entry starting with # is a comment, as it would be in a .gitignore file, and \# escapes it.
  • The patterns are read relative to the package's root, as git reads core.excludesFile, below every .gitignore file of the tree in precedence. The Membership Rule states how they combine with the tree's other exclusions.
  • Each pattern is normalized to NFC before it is matched, as the membership rule normalizes every pattern, so a pattern written in decomposed form matches the same names as one written composed.

docs.title: The [dependencies] Section
docs.text:
Implementation status

Dependency declaration is committed design. This section is the contract implementations are brought into conformance with — the same forward-contract convention the Library Crate Format uses for its unrealized sections. Conformance is asserted against this document as each piece lands.

Each entry in [dependencies] declares a dependency on another MTHDS package. The key is the alias — a snake_case identifier used in cross-package references (-> syntax).

[dependencies]
docproc     = { address = "github.com/mthds/document-processing", version = "^1.0.0" }
scoring_lib = { address = "github.com/mthds/scoring-lib", version = "^0.5.0" }

docs.title: Dependency Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description address string Yes The dependency's package address. MUST follow the hostname/path pattern. version string Yes Version constraint for the dependency (see Version Constraint Syntax). path string No Local filesystem path to the dependency, resolved relative to the manifest directory. For development-time workflows.

docs.title: Alias Rules
docs.text:
• The alias (the TOML key) MUST be snake_case, matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]*.
  • All aliases within a single [dependencies] section MUST be unique.
  • The alias is used in cross-package references: alias->domain.name.

docs.title: The path Field
docs.text:
When path is set, the dependency is resolved from the local filesystem instead of being fetched via VCS. This supports development-time workflows where packages are co-located on disk, similar to Cargo's path dependencies or Go's replace directives.

  • The path is resolved relative to the directory containing METHODS.toml.
  • Local path dependencies are NOT resolved transitively — only the root package's local paths are honored.
  • Local path dependencies are excluded from the lock file.

Example:

[dependencies]
scoring = { address = "github.com/mthds/scoring-lib", version = "^0.5.0", path = "../scoring-lib" }

docs.title: Version Constraint Syntax
docs.text:
Version constraints specify which versions of a dependency are acceptable.

Form Syntax Example Meaning Exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH 1.0.0 Exactly this version. Caret ^MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ^1.0.0 Compatible release (same major version). Tilde ~MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ~1.0.0 Approximately compatible (same major.minor). Greater-or-equal >=MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH >=1.0.0 This version or newer. Less-than <MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH <2.0.0 Older than this version. Greater >MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH >1.0.0 Newer than this version. Less-or-equal <=MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH <=2.0.0 This version or older. Equal ==MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ==1.0.0 Exactly this version. Not-equal !=MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH !=1.0.0 Any version except this one. Compound constraint , constraint >=1.0.0, <2.0.0 Both constraints must be satisfied. Wildcard *, MAJOR.*, MAJOR.MINOR.* 1.* Any version matching the prefix.

Partial versions are allowed: 1.0 is equivalent to 1.0.*.

Constraints are read as floors. Version resolution follows Minimum Version Selection: the resolver selects the lowest version that satisfies every constraint declared for a package across the dependency graph. A declared constraint therefore states the minimum a dependent is known to work with — its floor — and the resolved version is, for plain floor constraints, the maximum of the declared floors. Upper bounds and exclusions still narrow the admissible set, but a newly published version is never adopted merely for being newer: it becomes eligible only when some manifest raises a floor to it.

docs.title: The [exports] Section
docs.text:
The [exports] section controls which pipes are visible to consumers of the package.

Default visibility rules:

  • Concepts are always public. Concepts are vocabulary — they are always accessible from outside the package.
  • Pipes are private by default. A pipe not listed in [exports] is an implementation detail, invisible to consumers.
  • main_pipe is auto-exported. A pipe designated as main_pipe — in the manifest's [package] section or in a bundle header — is exported by virtue of being main_pipe, whether or not it also appears in [exports]. The export surface of a package is the union of [exports] and its auto-exported main pipes.

docs.title: Exports Table Structure
docs.text:
The [exports] section uses nested TOML tables that mirror the domain hierarchy. The domain path maps directly to the TOML table path:

[exports.legal]
pipes = ["classify_document"]

[exports.legal.contracts]
pipes = ["extract_clause", "analyze_nda", "compare_contracts"]

[exports.scoring]
pipes = ["compute_weighted_score"]

Each leaf table contains:

Field Type Required Description pipes array of strings Yes Pipe codes that are public from this domain. Each entry MUST be a valid pipe code (snake_case).

Validation rules:

  • Domain paths in [exports] MUST be valid domain codes.
  • Domain paths in [exports] MUST NOT start with a reserved domain segment (native, mthds, pipelex).
  • A domain MAY have both a pipes list and sub-domain tables (e.g., [exports.legal] with pipes AND [exports.legal.contracts]).

docs.title: Standalone Bundles (No Manifest)
docs.text:
A .mthds file without a METHODS.toml manifest is a standalone bundle. It behaves as an implicit local package with:

  • No dependencies (beyond native concepts).
  • All pipes treated as public (no visibility restrictions).
  • No package address (not distributable).

This preserves the "single file = working method" experience for learning, prototyping, and simple projects.

A method with no manifest is either a directory a caller hands over, whose method tree is rooted at that directory, or a .mthds file named alone, whose method tree is that one file and nothing else, so a file reference from it to any file beside it is refused. See Method Tree: The Root.

docs.title: Package Directory Structure
docs.text:
A package is a directory containing a METHODS.toml manifest and one or more .mthds bundle files. The directory layout follows a progressive enhancement principle — start minimal, add structure as needed.

Minimal package:

my_tool/
├── METHODS.toml
└── main.mthds

Full package:

legal_tools/
├── METHODS.toml
├── methods.lock
├── general_legal.mthds
├── contract_analysis.mthds
├── shareholder_agreements.mthds
├── scoring.mthds
├── requirements.txt
├── funcs/
│   └── scoring.py
├── templates/
│   └── nda_report.html
├── README.md
└── LICENSE

Rules:

  • METHODS.toml MUST be at the directory root, which is the root of the package's method tree.
  • methods.lock MUST be at the directory root, alongside METHODS.toml.
  • .mthds files MAY be at the root or in subdirectories. A compliant implementation MUST load every .mthds file of the method tree, and only those: a bundle the membership rule excludes is not part of the package.
  • Every file of the method tree belongs to the package and travels with it, whether a step reads it, such as a Python module or a template, or it is carried for people and agents, such as a README.md.
  • A single directory SHOULD contain one package. A repository MAY host several packages in subdirectories — a library repository — in which case each package is identified by its own manifest, and a specific package is located by manifest identity, never by directory path (see Distribution: Locating a Package Inside a Clone). A package in a directory below another package's root is out of that package's method tree, by the membership rule's nested-package default, so packages never hold one another.
  • The directory name is not part of the package's identity and MAY differ from the manifest name (see Name).

docs.title: Manifest Discovery
docs.text:
When loading a .mthds bundle, a compliant implementation SHOULD discover the manifest by walking up from the bundle file's directory, or from the directory a caller hands over:

  1. Check the current directory for METHODS.toml.
  2. If not found, move to the parent directory.
  3. Stop when METHODS.toml is found, an entry named .git of any kind is encountered (a directory, a file such as the one a submodule or a worktree holds, or a symbolic link, never followed), which is the entry that marks a nested repository under the membership rule, or the filesystem root is reached.
  4. If no manifest is found, the bundle is treated as a standalone bundle (no package).

The directory where discovery finds METHODS.toml is the root of the method's tree. When discovery finds none, the root is the directory handed over, or, for a .mthds file named alone, the tree is that one file (see Method Tree: The Root).

docs.title: Complete Manifest Example
docs.text:
[package]
name          = "nda_analyzer"
address       = "github.com/acme/legal-tools"
display_name  = "Legal Tools"
version       = "0.3.0"
description   = "Legal document analysis and contract review methods."
authors       = ["ACME Legal Tech <legal@acme.com>"]
license       = "MIT"
mthds_version = ">=8.0.0"
main_pipe     = "analyze_nda"
exclude       = ["drafts/"]

[exports.legal]
pipes = ["classify_document"]

[exports.legal.contracts]
pipes = ["extract_clause", "analyze_nda", "compare_contracts"]

[exports.scoring]
pipes = ["compute_weighted_score"]
Copy Markdown

docs.title: Method Tree
docs.text:
A method is a tree of files. Its bundles, its manifest, the Python modules its PipeFunc steps call, the templates and images its steps read, its requirements.txt and its README.md are all files of one tree, each named by its path from the tree's root, and the tree as a whole is identified by its digest. This page defines that object once: where the root is, which files belong, how a file is named and how one file names another, the digest, the file entry that carries a file from one program to another, and how a method declares its Python.

invoices/
├── METHODS.toml
├── README.md
├── main.mthds
├── requirements.txt
├── inputs.json           (the inputs of the last run)
├── examples/
│   └── invoice-inputs.json
├── funcs/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── totals.py
│   └── __pycache__/
├── templates/
│   ├── letter.html
│   └── logo.png
├── results/
│   ├── .gitignore        (holds the single pattern *)
│   └── run-1.json
├── .gitignore
└── .venv/

The method tree of this directory is:

METHODS.toml
README.md
examples/invoice-inputs.json
funcs/__init__.py
funcs/totals.py
main.mthds
requirements.txt
templates/letter.html
templates/logo.png

.gitignore and .venv/ are out because their names start with a dot, funcs/__pycache__/ and inputs.json are out by default, and results/run-1.json is out because the .gitignore file in its directory ignores every file there. Every other file belongs to the tree and travels with the method, whether a step reads it or it is carried for people and agents to read, examples/invoice-inputs.json included, since only a file named inputs.json or inputs.toml is kept out.

Implementation status

The method tree is committed design. This page is the contract implementations are brought into conformance with — the same forward-contract convention the Library Crate Format uses for its unrealized sections. Conformance is asserted against this document as each piece lands.

docs.title: The Root
docs.text:
A method tree is the set of regular files under a root directory that the membership rule admits, each named by its tree path from the root. The root is the directory holding METHODS.toml. A compliant implementation finds it from what a caller hands over:

  • A directory. The root is the nearest directory at or above the directory handed over that holds METHODS.toml, found by Manifest Discovery. When there is none, the method has no manifest, and the directory handed over is its root.
  • A .mthds file named alone. The root is the nearest directory at or above the file's own directory that holds METHODS.toml, found the same way. When there is none, the tree is that one file, under its file name, and nothing beside it is read: no .gitignore file and no pyvenv.cfg entry, beside it or above it, applies to it, so of the membership rule only the dot-segment rule reaches it. A file reference from it to any other file is refused, with a message saying to run the method's directory or to add a METHODS.toml.

A .mthds file named alone that the membership rule keeps out of its own tree is refused, naming the rule that excludes it: with no manifest, only a name starting with a dot does so, and when a METHODS.toml makes a root, so does any other part of the rule, such as a .gitignore file under that root that ignores the file.

Sending a directory is always the caller's explicit act. A .mthds file named alone never carries the files beside it unless a manifest makes their directory a method's root, so a bundle saved among unrelated documents never takes them anywhere.

A run loads one root tree and the trees of the packages it depends on, each with its own root and its own digest (see Dependencies Are Trees of Their Own).

A method's files are its own: they are authored once, travel with the method, and are its identity. A file a caller supplies for one run reaches the run as an input, a stuff in the wire form of the CLI I/O Contract, and is never a file of the tree.

docs.title: The Membership Rule
docs.text:
A regular file under the root belongs to the tree unless one of the following excludes it, and a directory that one of them excludes is excluded with everything under it:

  1. A path segment starting with a dot. This keeps out .git/, .venv/, .env, .gitignore, the .mthds/ directory where a project keeps its installed packages, and every other dotfile and dot directory, the state of editors and tools included. It is the rule that keeps the commonest secret files out by construction.
  2. The defaults. A directory named __pycache__ or node_modules; any directory holding an entry named pyvenv.cfg that is a regular file or a symbolic link, the link never followed, since PEP 405 places a pyvenv.cfg file at the top of every Python virtual environment, so a virtual environment stays out whatever its name, while a directory named pyvenv.cfg marks nothing; any directory below the root holding an entry named .git of any kind, a directory, a file such as the one a submodule or a worktree holds, or a symbolic link, never followed, whatever that entry holds and whether or not git would take it for a repository, so a nested repository stays out, as git leaves it out of every commit; and any directory below the root holding a file named METHODS.toml, so a nested package stays out, since it is another package and travels as a tree of its own (see Dependencies Are Trees of Their Own). The pyvenv.cfg default applies to the root too, so a root that is itself a virtual environment holds an empty tree, which no surface accepts. The root's own METHODS.toml is the manifest that makes it the root, and it excludes nothing. One default excludes a file rather than a directory: an entry named inputs.json or inputs.toml, at any depth, that is a regular file or a symbolic link, the link never followed, is a run's inputs file and stays out (see Run Inputs Files), while a directory of either name excludes nothing.
  3. The tree's own .gitignore files. The patterns of every .gitignore file inside the root, at any depth, read with git's own semantics as gitignore documents them: a pattern applies relative to the directory of the file that holds it, a deeper file's patterns take precedence over a shallower one's, git never descends into an excluded directory, and so a negation cannot re-include a file under an excluded directory. A .gitignore file is read as UTF-8, skipping a leading byte order mark as git skips it, and one whose bytes are not UTF-8 is an error naming its path, never skipped silently, as a symbolic link is. A .gitignore file inside an excluded directory is never read, so it is never an error. A pattern is normalized to NFC before it is matched, so a pattern an editor wrote in decomposed form matches the same names as one written composed, and it then matches tree paths byte for byte, letter case included, as git matches with core.ignoreCase off, whatever the file system. Only these files count: neither a user's global excludes, nor a repository's info/exclude, nor a .gitignore file above the root, so the same directory yields the same tree on every machine.
  4. The manifest's exclude patterns. The patterns of [package] exclude, in the same syntax and normalized to NFC in the same way, read as git reads core.excludesFile: relative to the root, and below every .gitignore file in precedence, so a negation in a .gitignore file can re-include a file they exclude. They keep out of the tree what a method wants kept out of the tree but not out of git.

No pattern re-includes a file that the dot-segment rule or a default excludes. A default looks at a directory's own entries whatever the patterns say of them, so a pattern that ignores a nested .git entry, a pyvenv.cfg entry or a nested METHODS.toml file does not bring its directory back.

The rule is deliberately close to what git would commit from the directory. A package is published by pushing a tag, so honouring the tree's own .gitignore files makes a local run, a run on a remote runner and a run of the published package see the same files.

docs.title: Symbolic Links and Other Entries
docs.text: A symbolic link that the membership rule does not exclude is an error naming its path: it is never followed and never skipped silently, since a link is either a mistake or a reach outside the root, and both deserve to be seen. Exclusion prunes first, so a link inside an excluded directory is never visited, and a link the rule excludes is no error. An entry that is neither a regular file, nor a directory, nor a symbolic link, such as a named pipe or a device, is an error naming its path in the same way.

docs.title: Run Artifacts Beside a Method
docs.text: A tool that creates a directory under a method's root to write its own files into, such as the results of a run, SHOULD make that directory self-excluding by writing into it a .gitignore file holding the single pattern *. The directory then stays out of the tree and out of git, and neither this rule nor its defaults need to know the directory's name.

docs.title: Run Inputs Files
docs.text:
A tool that runs a method from a directory may read the run's inputs from a file in that directory, as a command line reads the inputs.json it auto-detects in directory mode. That file holds one run's real data, which is never a file of the tree (see The Root), and if it were a member, sending or saving the method would carry that data along and store it as method content. The directory a tool runs need not be the root, since a METHODS.toml above it makes the root higher up, so the defaults keep a file named inputs.json or inputs.toml out of every tree at any depth. Because the exclusion belongs to the membership rule rather than to each client's own choice, every program that lists the tree leaves the file out alike, so the tree a client sends, the tree a runtime lists and the tree a save records keep one digest.

Nothing in this standard reads inputs.toml. A runtime MAY auto-detect an inputs file written in TOML beside the JSON one, and the rule keeps both spellings out, so the format a tool reads never decides whether a run's data travels with the method.

A tool MAY still read an inputs file as a run's inputs: the file never travels with the tree, so reading it carries nothing into the method. A method that ships example inputs for people and agents to read gives them any other name, such as examples/invoice-inputs.json, and they are then ordinary members of the tree.

docs.title: Checking the Rule Against Git
docs.text:
Because the membership rule follows git, git itself can produce the expected listing of a test tree, which keeps an implementation from sharing a misreading of git's semantics with the person who wrote its tests. In a scratch repository holding the test tree, with global and system configuration turned off, core.ignoreCase set to false, and core.excludesFile holding the case's exclude patterns one per line, git -c core.ignoreCase=false ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z lists the files git would commit. Setting core.ignoreCase matters on a case-insensitive file system, where git init writes core.ignoreCase = true into the scratch repository's own configuration and git then matches every pattern regardless of case, so that *.PY would exclude a.py, whereas the membership rule matches tree paths byte for byte. Git also matches a pattern as it is written against a name as the file system holds it, so every pattern goes into the scratch repository, in its .gitignore files and in core.excludesFile, normalized to NFC, as the membership rule normalizes it before matching, and every file and directory of the scratch tree is written under its name in NFC, as the membership rule reads it. A test whose point is a name stored on disk in decomposed form is therefore checked without git as its oracle. Git applies the patterns and nothing else, so the dot-segment rule and the defaults are applied after its listing, which gives the same result because no pattern re-includes what they exclude and a .gitignore file inside an excluded directory reaches nothing outside it. Dropping from git's output every path holding a segment that starts with a dot, every path inside a __pycache__ or node_modules directory, every path whose last segment is inputs.json or inputs.toml, which git lists alike for a regular file and for a symbolic link, and every path at or inside a directory holding an entry named pyvenv.cfg that is a file or a symbolic link, a directory below the root holding an entry named .git, or a directory below the root holding METHODS.toml gives the tree's listing. These last three defaults are read from the test tree itself rather than from git's output, since git never lists a .git entry and a pattern may keep out of that output the very file that triggers the other two.

The nested repository default is where the membership rule and git part ways. Git leaves a directory out as a nested repository only when its .git entry leads to a repository, and lists as untracked the files under a directory whose .git entry is an empty directory, or a file that names no repository, such as one whose gitdir: line points nowhere. The membership rule excludes any directory below the root holding an entry named .git of any kind, whatever it holds, so the files git lists under such a directory are dropped with the rest.

docs.title: Tree Paths
docs.text:
A tree path names a file of a tree from its root, such as templates/letter.html:

  • It is a relative POSIX path: segments separated by /, with no leading or trailing / and no empty segment.
  • No segment is . or .., and no segment holds a backslash (\), a colon (:), or a control character, meaning any character of Unicode general category Cc, NUL and the line breaks among them.
  • It is encoded as UTF-8 in Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC), and tree paths are compared, sorted and matched byte for byte on that encoding.
  • Each segment is at most 255 bytes long and the whole path at most 1024 bytes long, in that encoding.

Two tree paths collide when their case foldings are equal. The case folding of a tree path takes two steps: the path in NFC is mapped by Unicode full case folding, which replaces each character holding an entry of status C or F in the CaseFolding.txt of Unicode 14.0 or of any later version by that entry's mapping, with no locale tailoring, and the result is normalized to NFC again. In Python it is nfc(nfc(p).casefold()), where nfc is unicodedata.normalize("NFC", …). Implementations reading different versions of the file may differ only on characters assigned after Unicode 14.0. Case folding is what a case-insensitive file system compares names by, and it reaches further than converting to lowercase: ß collides with SS, ẞ with ß, ς with σ, and ſ with s. JavaScript has no built-in full case folding, toLowerCase being a case conversion and not a folding, so an implementation written in it carries the folding table itself.

Within one tree, no two paths collide and no path collides with a directory of another: one tree never holds both README.md and readme.md, nor both straße.txt and STRASSE.txt, nor both templates and templates/letter.html, nor both Templates and templates/letter.html. A tree written out on a case-insensitive file system therefore loses no file and never needs a file and a directory under one name.

A name listed from a file system is normalized to NFC, since some file systems hand back a decomposed form of an accented name, and two names in one directory that are equal after normalization are refused, naming both. A tree path given as text rather than listed, such as a key of a map of file entries, is never normalized: one not already in NFC is not a tree path. A file reference is not a tree path but names one, and is normalized as it is resolved. A path that breaks any rule above is refused, naming it.

The membership rule applies before these rules, so a name it excludes is never checked against them: a name that breaks them is excluded silently, whether the rule excludes it directly, as a pattern naming it does, or it lies inside an excluded directory.

A tree path is a name, never a storage location. A receiver that stores a file keeps it under its hash, as the file entry carries it, so a tree path may hold accents, spaces or a non-Latin script, and no storage system's naming rules reach an author.

docs.title: File References
docs.text:
A file reference is a relative path, written in a file of a tree, that names another file of the same tree. It is written in one of two contexts:

  • Path context: a field of a bundle that names a file, whose whole value is the reference's path. Every field that names a method file, whether this specification defines it or an implementation adds it, is a file reference in path context and follows this rule.
  • URL context: a relative URL inside a template, such as the src of an image in an HTML template, whose path is what is left once its query and its fragment are dropped, since they take no part. Only a relative URL with a path is a file reference. A URL that names a scheme, such as https:, data: or mailto:, one that holds an authority, such as //host/x, and one with no path, such as #top, ?v=2 or an empty one, are not file references: each is left exactly as written and never refused.
letters/
├── METHODS.toml
├── shared/
│   └── logo.png
└── templates/
    └── letter.html       (holds <img src="../shared/logo.png">)

A file reference is resolved against the directory of the file that holds it, as a relative URL is resolved in a web page, and is refused in one of four ways: as a malformed reference, written in a form a file reference never takes; as not a tree path, when it is empty or names a file in a way no tree path can, such as with an empty segment or a trailing /; as leaving the tree, when it climbs above the root; or as not in the tree, when the tree holds no file at the path it resolves to. The steps run in this order, and a reference that fails more than one check is refused by the first step that fails:

  1. Take its path, as its context defines it. In path context, an empty reference is refused as not a tree path.
  2. Check its form. A reference is written with / separators, so it is refused as malformed when its path holds a backslash or is absolute, starting with /, and, in path context, when it names a scheme or holds an authority.
  3. Decode it. In URL context, the path is split into segments at each / before each segment is percent-decoded, so decoding never creates a separator. A segment whose decoding yields a /, a \, a control character, or bytes that are not UTF-8 makes the reference malformed, and so does a % not followed by two hexadecimal digits, as in logo%2.png or 100%.png. A reference in path context is never percent-decoded.
  4. Normalize it to NFC, so a reference an editor wrote in decomposed form names the same file as one written composed.
  5. Resolve it. Take the directory of the holding file's tree path, which is the root for a file at the root, join the path to it with /, and normalize the result lexically: drop each . segment, and let each .. segment remove the segment before it. A .. that would climb above the root is refused as leaving the tree.
  6. Check the result. A result naming the root, with no segment or with only a trailing /, as ../ held by templates/letter.html resolves to, is the root itself, which this step lets through to the next, where it is refused as not in the tree, its resolved path named .. Any other result that is not a tree path, such as one holding an empty segment, as images/ does by ending in / after a name, is refused as not a tree path. The check reads the resolved path, so a//b is refused, while a//../b resolves to a/b, its .. having removed the empty segment before it.
  7. Look it up. The result MUST name a file of the tree. A result at which the tree holds no file is refused as not in the tree, and so is one naming a directory of the tree, as images/. resolves to images, or the root itself, as a/.. does, whose resolved path is named ..

In the example, ../shared/logo.png held by templates/letter.html resolves to shared/logo.png.

Resolving a reference is a lookup in the tree's set of paths, never a file system access. A reference can only name a file the tree holds, which is what makes .. harmless, and no implementation opens a path that a method's author, or a caller, wrote.

A reference refused as not in the tree names the reference and the path it resolved to, written . when that is the root. An implementation that listed the tree from a directory also names the rule that excluded the file, when one did, and for a file inside a nested repository or a nested package it names that directory, so an author who meant to ship the file learns why it is not in the tree. In the one-file tree of a .mthds file named alone, the refusal says to run the method's directory or to add a METHODS.toml. That advice belongs to this refusal alone: a reference from a one-file tree that fails an earlier step is refused by that step, as malformed, as not a tree path or as leaving the tree, like any other.

docs.title: The Tree Digest
docs.text:
The tree digest identifies a tree by its bytes. It is sha256: followed by the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 of the tree's listing, which holds one line per file of the tree, sorted by tree path byte for byte, each line being exactly what sha256sum prints for that file: the SHA-256 of the file's bytes in lowercase hexadecimal, two spaces, the file's tree path, and a line feed.

mkdir -p greetings/funcs greetings/templates && cd greetings
printf '# Greetings\n' > README.md
printf 'domain = "greetings"\n' > main.mthds
printf 'def shout(text):\n    return text.upper()\n' > funcs/text_utils.py
printf '<p>Hello</p>\n' > templates/card.html

The listing of this tree is:

af12591480ada38cf107d1a76bc5e2e111ad4c7ec5f3a2a63d058f5f5ab6b91c  README.md
d78fff51f2aea9cb634456d3c83925ae047d967798f28e8a4b3e7b232a1dc097  funcs/text_utils.py
45b0d6a4796412598db6d328978990fc44563e59057d6e3bfc8419ae3ed3981f  main.mthds
3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0  templates/card.html

and its digest is sha256:801fca61b41566e46d3fb1923e323590da7a539fd3e7af7455e7cba3934d4674.

The encoding is injective: a hash has a fixed width and a tree path holds no line break, so two different trees never share a listing.

docs.title: The Reference Pipeline
docs.text:
Anyone can recompute a digest with coreutils. Given the tree's paths, one per line, sort them in the C locale, pass each to sha256sum, and pass the listing to sha256sum once more:

cd greetings
printf '%s\n' README.md funcs/text_utils.py main.mthds templates/card.html \
  | LC_ALL=C sort \
  | while IFS= read -r f; do sha256sum -- "$f"; done \
  | sha256sum
# 801fca61b41566e46d3fb1923e323590da7a539fd3e7af7455e7cba3934d4674  -

LC_ALL=C is what makes sort order the paths byte for byte. Under another locale it orders them differently, here funcs/text_utils.py, main.mthds, README.md, templates/card.html, and the digest it gives is wrong. shasum -a 256 prints the same line format as sha256sum and can stand in for it. A conformance corpus takes its expected digests from this pipeline rather than from any implementation.

docs.title: Digest and Fingerprint
docs.text: The tree digest and the library crate fingerprint answer different questions. The digest changes with any byte of any file and with any tree path, comments and formatting included, so it says whether two trees hold the same files. The fingerprint changes only when what the method means changes, so it says whether two methods do the same thing. The lock file records both for each dependency.

docs.title: The File Entry
docs.text:
A file entry is how one file of a tree travels from one program to another, under its tree path, as its bytes or as their hash. A tree travels as a map from tree path to file entry:

{
  "README.md": "# Greetings\n",
  "main.mthds": "domain = \"greetings\"\n",
  "funcs/text_utils.py": { "base64": "ZGVmIHNob3V0KHRleHQpOgogICAgcmV0dXJuIHRleHQudXBwZXIoKQo=" },
  "templates/card.html": {
    "sha256": "3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0",
    "size": 13
  }
}

This map carries the greetings tree above, so its digest is sha256:801fca61b41566e46d3fb1923e323590da7a539fd3e7af7455e7cba3934d4674 whichever form each file travels in. An entry takes exactly one of three forms:

  • A string is the file's text: the file's bytes are the UTF-8 encoding of the string, exactly, with no line ending converted and no byte order mark added. A string holding a code point that UTF-8 cannot encode, such as a lone surrogate, is refused. This is the shorthand that keeps the commonest case, a bundle pasted as text, a one-liner.
  • { "base64": "…" } carries any bytes, encoded with the standard Base64 alphabet of RFC 4648, padded, with no line breaks, and canonical as RFC 4648 defines it: the pad bits, which the last character before the = padding carries beyond the encoded bytes, are zero. An encoding that breaks any of these, non-zero pad bits included, is not valid Base64, and its entry is refused.
  • { "sha256": "…", "size": … } names bytes the receiver already holds: sha256 is their SHA-256 in lowercase hexadecimal and size their length in bytes, a JSON integer written without a fraction or an exponent, so a size written 13.0 is refused. It resolves only in the receiver's own blob store, and a receiver that does not hold those bytes, or holds them with another size, refuses the entry, naming the hash.

An entry object holds no other key and no key twice, and no entry names a file by URL: a URL form would let a sender point the receiver at an address of its choosing, which is exactly what reading only the files it is sent prevents.

A map of entries is refused, naming the offending path, when one of its keys:

  • is not a tree path, which a key not already in NFC is not, since a receiver refuses such a key rather than normalize it, so two keys equal after normalization never both stand; or holds a segment that the membership rule's dot-segment rule or its name defaults exclude (a segment starting with a dot, a __pycache__ or node_modules directory, or a file named pyvenv.cfg, inputs.json or inputs.toml), or names a file METHODS.toml anywhere but at the root, since no tree has such a member;
  • is given twice in the document, as written or once its JSON escapes are decoded, which a receiver detects in the text it parses rather than keeping one of the values, or holds an entry object that gives one of its own keys twice, which is refused in the same way;
  • collides with another key, or with a directory of another key, such as readme.md beside README.md, STRASSE.txt beside straße.txt, or Templates beside templates/letter.html.

A map with no key is refused: a tree holds at least one file.

The same map is the method source of a request under the HTTP Runner Protocol, where a runner that keeps a blob store also lets a sender upload once the files it lacks and send the rest by hash. A map has no order, so no file of it is "the first": a request that names no pipe starts at the method's main_pipe, as the protocol states.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The standard bounds a tree path's length and nothing else. Each implementation bounds as its own policy a file's size, a tree's file count and its total size, and the total of a request's inline entries, and refuses a tree past one of them with a message naming the limit. A program listing a tree for a receiver whose limits it knows SHOULD count files and sum their sizes as it walks the directory, and stop at the first limit passed, before hashing any file, with a message naming the root, the limit and the count reached, so that a directory handed over by mistake is refused in moments rather than read in full.

docs.title: Python Modules
docs.text: A PipeFunc names its function by its Python import path from the root of the tree that holds the bundle, which is the import root: function_name = "funcs.text_utils.shout" names the function shout of the module funcs/text_utils.py of the greetings tree, and the modules that one imports are resolved from the same root. The name is normalized to NFC before it is mapped to a module's tree path, as a file reference is at step 4, so a name written in decomposed form finds its module, and each of its segments must be a Python identifier that NFKC normalization leaves unchanged, since Python reads identifiers in NFKC and would otherwise import another file than the tree holds. The rule is the PipeFunc field's own, with an example of each.

docs.title: Python Dependencies: requirements.txt
docs.text:
A method whose Python needs third-party packages declares them in a file named requirements.txt at the root of its tree:

# The packages funcs/totals.py imports
pandas>=2.2,<3
openpyxl==3.1.5
tzdata; python_version >= "3.12"

Each line is blank, a comment whose first character other than a space or a tab is #, or exactly one requirement written as PEP 508 defines it, environment markers included. A requirement naming a URL (name @ https://…), an option of any kind (a line starting with -, such as -e, -r, -c or --index-url), a comment after a requirement, and a line continued with a backslash are refused, naming the line. Only the root's requirements.txt declares anything: a file of that name elsewhere in the tree is an ordinary file.

The standard specifies the file and nothing about how it is satisfied. A runtime decides how to satisfy it, and a runtime that cannot, such as one whose environment lacks a declared package or holds it at a version the requirement excludes, SHOULD refuse the method when it loads, naming each package it cannot satisfy, rather than fail later inside a function.

docs.title: Dependencies Are Trees of Their Own
docs.text:
A package a method depends on is a tree of its own, with its own root and its own digest, and never travels inside the tree that depends on it. The .mthds/ directory where a project keeps its installed packages starts with a dot, so it is out of every tree, and a package kept in a directory below another package's root is out of that package's tree by the nested-package default, so the packages of a library repository never hold one another.

  • A dependency with a local path is the method tree rooted at that directory, listed under the membership rule like any other.
  • A fetched dependency's tree is the set of files of the package's directory in the commit its resolved version points at, read from the commit's git objects as stored, with no checkout filter, no line-ending conversion and no export-ignore attribute applied, so its digest is the same on every machine, and filtered by the membership rule, reading the .gitignore files that commit holds inside the package's directory and the package's own exclude patterns. A file committed despite a pattern that matches it is therefore out of the published tree as it is out of the local one, a submodule contributes no file, and a symbolic link committed in the package's directory is an error naming its path unless the rule excludes it.

A tree written out is read back as written. A copy of a tree that a program writes to disk, such as a package in a cache, holds the tree's files at their tree paths and nothing else, and those files are the tree: a reader takes every file of the copy as a file of the tree and never applies the membership rule to it again. The rule cannot be applied twice, since the .gitignore files that shaped the tree start with a dot and are left out of the copy, so a manifest exclude pattern that one of them overrode with a negation would exclude its file a second time.

The lock file records each fetched dependency's tree digest, which an install checks against the tree it fetched.

docs.title: .mthds File Format
docs.text: The .mthds file is a TOML document that defines typed data (concepts) and typed transformations (pipes) within a single domain. This page is the normative reference for every field, validation rule, and structural constraint of the format.

docs.title: File Encoding and Syntax
docs.text: A .mthds file MUST be a valid TOML document encoded in UTF-8. The file extension MUST be .mthds. Parsers MUST reject files that are not valid TOML before any MTHDS-specific validation occurs.

docs.title: Top-Level Structure
docs.text:
A .mthds file is called a bundle. It consists of:

  1. Header fields — top-level key-value pairs that identify the bundle.
  2. Concept definitions — a [concept] table and/or [concept.<ConceptCode>] sub-tables.
  3. Pipe definitions — [pipe.<pipe_code>] sub-tables.

All three sections are optional in the TOML sense (an empty .mthds file is valid TOML), but a useful bundle will contain at least one concept or one pipe.

docs.title: Header Fields
docs.text:
Header fields appear at the top level of the TOML document, before any [concept] or [pipe] tables.

Field Type Required Description domain string Yes The domain this bundle belongs to. Determines the namespace for all concepts and pipes defined in this file. description string No A human-readable description of what this bundle provides. system_prompt string No A default system prompt applied to all PipeLLM pipes in this bundle that do not define their own system_prompt. main_pipe string No The pipe code of the bundle's primary entry point. If set, this pipe is auto-exported when the bundle is part of a package.

Validation rules:

  • domain MUST be a valid domain code (see Domain Naming Rules).
  • main_pipe, if present, MUST be a valid pipe code (snake_case) and MUST reference a pipe defined in this bundle.

Example:

domain      = "legal.contracts"
description = "Contract analysis methods for legal documents"
main_pipe   = "extract_clause"

docs.title: Domain Naming Rules
docs.text:
Domain codes define the namespace for all concepts and pipes in a bundle.

Syntax:

  • A domain code is one or more snake_case segments separated by . (dot).
  • Each segment MUST match the pattern [a-z][a-z0-9_]*.
  • Domains MAY be hierarchical: legal, legal.contracts, legal.contracts.shareholder.

Reserved domains:

The following domain names are reserved and MUST NOT be used as the first segment of any user-defined domain:

  • native — built-in concept types
  • mthds — reserved for the MTHDS standard
  • pipelex — reserved for the reference implementation

A compliant implementation MUST reject bundles that declare a domain starting with a reserved segment (e.g., native.custom is invalid).

Recommendations:

  • Depth SHOULD be 1–3 levels.
  • Each segment SHOULD be 1–4 words.

docs.title: Concept Definitions
docs.text: Concepts are typed data declarations. They define the vocabulary of a domain — the kinds of data that pipes accept and produce.

docs.title: Simple Concept Declarations
docs.text:
The simplest form of concept declaration uses a flat [concept] table where each key is a concept code and the value is a description string:

[concept]
ContractClause = "A clause extracted from a legal contract"
UserProfile    = "A user's profile information"

This form declares concepts with no structure and no refinement. They exist as named types.

docs.title: Structured Concept Declarations
docs.text:
A concept with fields uses a [concept.<ConceptCode>] sub-table:

[concept.LineItem]
description = "A single line item in an invoice"

[concept.LineItem.structure]
product_name = { type = "text", description = "Name of the product", required = true }
quantity     = { type = "integer", description = "Quantity ordered", required = true }
unit_price   = { type = "number", description = "Price per unit", required = true }

Both forms MAY coexist in the same bundle. A bundle MAY mix simple declarations in [concept] with structured declarations as [concept.<Code>] sub-tables.

docs.title: Concept Blueprint Fields
docs.text:
When using the structured form [concept.<ConceptCode>], the following fields are available:

Field Type Required Description description string Yes Human-readable description of the concept. structure table or string No Field definitions for the concept. If a string, it is a shorthand description (equivalent to a simple declaration). If a table, each key is a field name mapped to a field blueprint. refines string No A concept reference indicating that this concept is a specialization of another concept. hints table No Optional intent hints for the concept — non-normative presentation intent that applies wherever the concept is presented.

Validation rules:

  • refines and structure MUST NOT both be present on the same concept. A concept either refines another concept or defines its own structure, not both.
  • refines, if present, MUST be a valid concept reference: either a bare concept code (PascalCase) or a domain-qualified reference (domain.ConceptCode). Cross-package references (alias->domain.ConceptCode) are also valid.
  • Concept codes MUST be PascalCase, matching the pattern [A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*.
  • Concept codes MUST NOT collide with native concept codes (see Native Concepts).

docs.title: Concept Refinement
docs.text:
Refinement establishes a specialization relationship between concepts. A concept that refines another inherits its semantic meaning and can be used anywhere the parent concept is expected.

[concept.NonCompeteClause]
description = "A non-compete clause in an employment contract"
refines     = "ContractClause"

The refines field accepts:

  • A bare concept code: "ContractClause" — resolved within the current bundle's domain.
  • A domain-qualified reference: "legal.ContractClause" — resolved within the current package.
  • A cross-package reference: "acme_legal->legal.contracts.NonDisclosureAgreement" — resolved from a dependency.

docs.title: Concept Structure Fields
docs.text:
When structure is a table, each key is a field name and each value is a field blueprint. Field names MUST NOT start with an underscore (_), as these are reserved for internal use. Field names MUST NOT collide with reserved field names (Pydantic model attributes and internal metadata fields).

A field's value is either a field blueprint table or a bare string, which is shorthand for a required text field: summary = "A one-line summary" declares exactly what summary = { type = "text", required = true, description = "A one-line summary" } declares. The shorthand carries a description and nothing else, so a field needing any other key is written as a table.

docs.title: Field Blueprint
docs.text:
Each field in a concept structure is defined by a field blueprint:

Field Type Required Description description string Yes Human-readable description of the field. type string Conditional The field type. Required unless choices is provided. required boolean No Whether the field is required. Default: false. default_value any No Default value for the field. Must match the declared type. choices array of strings No Fixed set of allowed string values. When choices is set, type MUST be omitted (the type is implicitly an enum of the given choices). key_type string Conditional Key type for dict fields. Required when type = "dict". value_type string Conditional Value type for dict fields. Required when type = "dict". item_type string No Item type for list fields. When set to "concept", item_concept_ref is required. concept_ref string Conditional Concept reference for concept-typed fields. Required when type = "concept". item_concept_ref string Conditional Concept reference for list items when item_type = "concept". hints table No Optional intent hints for the field — non-normative presentation intent.

The keys of a field blueprint are a closed set, exactly like an input slot table's. A key this table does not define MUST be rejected — a hopeful key (minimum, examples, unit, …) that validated green would be silently dropped, and an author would have no way to learn the field never carried what they wrote.

docs.title: Field Types
docs.text:
The type field accepts the following values:

Type Description default_value type text A string value. string integer A whole number. integer number A numeric value (integer or floating-point). integer or float boolean A true/false value. boolean date A calendar date value. datetime datetime A date with a time of day (a point in time). datetime time A time of day, optionally with a UTC offset. time list An ordered collection. Use item_type to specify element type. array dict A key-value mapping. Requires key_type and value_type. table concept A reference to another concept. Requires concept_ref. Cannot have default_value. (not allowed)

When type is omitted and choices is provided, the field is an enumeration field. The value MUST be one of the strings in the choices array.

Validation rules for field types:

  • type = "dict": key_type and value_type MUST both be non-empty.
  • value_type = "Any" is a reserved marker declaring the dict's value type unspecified: the values are arbitrary, and a consumer surfaces the field as declared imprecision (e.g. dict[str, Any] with a caveat), never as a guessed value shape. It appears primarily in materialized native concept definitions; authors SHOULD declare a concrete value type instead.
  • type = "concept": concept_ref MUST be set. default_value MUST NOT be set.
  • type = "list" with item_type = "concept": item_concept_ref MUST be set.
  • item_concept_ref MUST NOT be set unless item_type = "concept".
  • concept_ref MUST NOT be set unless type = "concept".
  • If choices is provided and type is omitted, default_value (if present) MUST be one of the values in choices.
  • If both type and default_value are set, the runtime type of default_value MUST match the declared type.
  • A field MUST NOT declare both required = true and default_value. A default means "applied when the caller omits the field", which makes absence legal; required means "must be present". The pair is two contradictory instructions on one field, and it fails validation rather than resolving to whichever the implementation happens to check first.

Example — concept with all field types:

[concept.CandidateProfile]
description = "A candidate's profile for job matching"

[concept.CandidateProfile.structure]
full_name        = { type = "text", description = "Full name", required = true }
years_experience = { type = "integer", description = "Years of professional experience" }
gpa              = { type = "number", description = "Grade point average" }
is_active        = { type = "boolean", description = "Whether actively looking", default_value = true }
graduation_date  = { type = "date", description = "Date of graduation" }
last_seen_at     = { type = "datetime", description = "Last activity timestamp" }
preferred_slot   = { type = "time", description = "Preferred interview time of day" }
skills           = { type = "list", item_type = "text", description = "List of skills" }
metadata         = { type = "dict", key_type = "text", value_type = "text", description = "Additional metadata" }
seniority_level  = { description = "Seniority level", choices = ["junior", "mid", "senior", "lead"] }
address          = { type = "concept", concept_ref = "Address", description = "Home address" }
references       = { type = "list", item_type = "concept", item_concept_ref = "ContactInfo", description = "Professional references" }

docs.title: Native Concepts
docs.text:
Native concepts are built-in types that are always available in every bundle without declaration. They belong to the reserved native domain.

Code Qualified Reference Description Dynamic native.Dynamic A dynamically-typed value. Text native.Text A text string. Image native.Image An image (binary). Document native.Document A document (e.g., PDF, web page). Html native.Html HTML content. TextAndImages native.TextAndImages Combined text and image content. Number native.Number A numeric value. YesNo native.YesNo The answer to a yes/no question. Choice native.Choice One option picked out of a declared set. Rating native.Rating A position on an ordered scale of described levels. Date native.Date A calendar date, optionally with a time of day. Time native.Time A time of day, optionally with a UTC offset. Page native.Page A single page extracted from a document. JSON native.JSON A JSON value. SearchResult native.SearchResult A web search result with answer and sources. Anything native.Anything Accepts any type. Composite native.Composite A named composition of contents.

Native concepts MAY be referenced by bare code (Text, Image) or by qualified reference (native.Text, native.Image). Bare native concept codes always take priority during resolution.

A bundle MUST NOT declare a concept with the same code as a native concept. A compliant implementation MUST reject such declarations.

Each native concept's exact blueprint form — its fields, their types, and their descriptions — is pinned per standard version in Native Concept Definitions. Implementations MUST use the pinned definitions verbatim (no reflection over internal runtime types) wherever a native's structural definition is needed, such as library crate materialization.

docs.title: Pipe Definitions
docs.text: Pipes are typed transformations. Each pipe has a typed signature: it declares what concepts it accepts as input and what concept it produces as output.

docs.title: Common Pipe Fields
docs.text:
Concrete pipe types share these base fields:

Field Type Required Description type string Yes for concrete pipes The pipe type. Determines which category and additional fields are available. Omitted only for contract-only PipeSignature declarations. description string Yes Human-readable description of what this pipe does. inputs table No Input declarations. Keys are input names (plain snake_case), values are input slot declarations (see Input slot declarations). output string Yes The output concept reference with optional multiplicity.

Pipe codes:

  • Pipe codes are the keys in [pipe.<pipe_code>] tables.
  • Pipe codes MUST be snake_case, matching the pattern [a-z][a-z0-9_]*.

Input names:

  • An input name MUST be a plain snake_case identifier, matching the pattern [a-z][a-z0-9_]*, on every pipe, operator or controller alike. It names one whole value, of the concept its slot declares.
  • An input name MUST NOT contain a dot. A key such as "invoice.total" = "Number" does not declare a field of invoice: a compliant implementation MUST reject it, as it rejects any other name that is not a plain snake_case identifier (InvoiceTotal, 2nd_total), and SHOULD report the refusal as method.identifier_invalid.
  • A pipe that needs one field of a value receives it in one of two ways. Either it declares the root with its whole concept and reads the field through the root in its template (invoice = "Invoice", read as $invoice.total, see Inputs Read Through Templates), or the calling sequence hands it the field under a plain name with a binding step ({ from = "invoice.total", result = "total_amount" }, see Binding Steps) and the pipe declares total_amount = "Number". The message refusing a dotted name SHOULD name both remedies.
  • The names under which a step stores a value in working memory, such as a pipe step's result, take the same form, so that an input can read whatever a step stores (see Stored Names).

Concept references in inputs and output:

Concept references in inputs and output support an optional multiplicity suffix and, for pipe declarations only, a presence marker:

Syntax Meaning ConceptName A single instance. ConceptName[] A variable-length list (runtime determines count). ConceptName[N] A fixed-length list of exactly N items (N ≥ 2). ConceptName[1] A single instance — the same slot as ConceptName, with the count written out. Not a one-item list. ConceptName? Optional single value. The slot may resolve as a recorded absence. ConceptName! Forced single input. If the slot is absent at run time, the run fails loudly. Inputs only.

The bracketed count MUST be at least 1: ConceptName[0] is invalid, because a fixed count of zero declares a slot that can hold nothing. A count of exactly one is single throughout the standard — ConceptName[1] is a way of writing ConceptName, never a one-element list — so nothing downstream wraps such a value in an array, and a fixed count reported on any wire is always greater than one. Every artifact that carries multiplicity states the same rule: the library crate materializes it, and pipe I/O contracts, the input-form descriptor and the output-form descriptor report it.

Concept references MAY be bare codes (Text), domain-qualified (legal.ContractClause), or cross-package qualified (alias->domain.ConceptCode).

Presence markers have these constraints:

  • Markers apply only to pipe inputs and output, not concept definitions, refines, or structure fields.
  • Markers MUST NOT be combined with multiplicity. Concept[]?, Concept[N]?, Concept[]!, and Concept[N]! are invalid because plural slots use an empty list when no items are produced.
  • ! MUST NOT appear on output. A force marker is an input-side assertion.

Input slot declarations:

Each value in inputs declares one input slot, in one of two forms. The string form is a concept reference with optional multiplicity and presence marker, as specified above. The expanded form is a table:

[pipe.summarize]
type        = "PipeLLM"
description = "Summarize a contract, following optional steering instructions"
output      = "Summary"

[pipe.summarize.inputs]
contract     = "legal.Contract"
instructions = { concept = "Text?", hints = { intent = "prose" } }

Rules for the expanded form:

  • concept (string) is required and carries exactly the same grammar as the string form — a concept reference with optional multiplicity and optional presence marker. x = "S" and x = { concept = "S" } are equivalent.
  • hints (table) is optional and attaches intent hints to the slot.
  • No other keys are defined in this version of the standard. An unknown key in an input slot table MUST be rejected. (The form is deliberately shaped so that future versions can add per-slot authoring fields — such as a slot description — without a second syntax.)
  • The expanded form applies to inputs only. output is always a string.

Example:

[pipe.analyze_contract]
type        = "PipeLLM"
description = "Analyze a legal contract and extract key clauses"
output      = "ContractClause[5]"

[pipe.analyze_contract.inputs]
contract_text = "Text"

docs.title: Pipe Types
docs.text:
MTHDS defines pipe types in two categories:

Operators — pipes that perform a single transformation:

Type Value Description PipeLLM "PipeLLM" Generates output using a large language model. PipeStructure "PipeStructure" Turns text into a structured concept using a large language model. PipeFunc "PipeFunc" Calls a Python function of the method's tree. PipeImgGen "PipeImgGen" Generates images using an image generation model. PipeExtract "PipeExtract" Extracts structured content from documents. PipeSearch "PipeSearch" Searches the web and returns structured results. PipeJudge "PipeJudge" Asks a judging model one or several closed questions about the evidence its prompt presents, and returns a verdict for each. PipeCompose "PipeCompose" Composes output from templates or constructs.

Controllers — pipes that orchestrate other pipes:

Type Value Description PipeSequence "PipeSequence" Executes a series of pipes in order. PipeParallel "PipeParallel" Executes pipes concurrently. PipeCondition "PipeCondition" Routes execution based on a condition. PipeBatch "PipeBatch" Maps a pipe over each item in a list.

docs.title: Contract-Only Pipe Signatures
docs.text:
A [pipe.<pipe_code>] section with no type is a PipeSignature when it contains only contract fields:

Field Type Required Description description string Yes Human-readable description of the intended pipe. inputs table No Input declarations, in either input slot form — the string form, or the expanded form with hints. output string Yes Output concept reference. Multiplicity and ? are supported. signature_for string No Optional hint naming the concrete pipe type expected later, such as "PipeLLM".

PipeSignature is not a pipe type value. Authors MUST NOT write type = "PipeSignature". A typeless pipe section that contains implementation fields such as prompt, steps, branches, or model is invalid because concrete implementations must declare their type.

Example:

[pipe.summarize_doc]
description   = "Summarize a source document"
inputs        = { document = "Document" }
output        = "Text"
signature_for = "PipeLLM"

docs.title: Inputs Read Through Templates
docs.text:
PipeLLM, PipeImgGen, PipeSearch, PipeJudge and PipeCompose read their inputs through templates, and the validation rules of each operator name the fields that do the reading. For these five operators the input rule runs in both directions: every variable those fields reference MUST correspond to a declared input, apart from the names the operator's own rules exclude, and every declared input MUST be read by at least one of them. A declared input that no such field reads is rejected.

A template variable is a dotted path whose first segment, its root, names an input, and whose following segments, if any, name fields reached through that input's concept. A variable corresponds to the declared input its root names, and reads that input. The match is made by the root alone and is the same on every operator, a PipeJudge's questions and a PipeCompose construct's from paths included, with no per-operator exception:

  • $deal.customer_name reads the input deal.
  • @page.page_view and {{ page.page_view.url }} read the input page, declared with its whole concept (page = "Page"). The field is reached through the root in the template and is never declared as an input of its own, since an input name is a plain name.
  • An optional (?) input is not exempt. A conditional reference such as @?note or {% if note %}…{% endif %} reads it.

A variable's value and its concept are what its path reaches through the root's declared concept. Each segment after the root names a field of the concept reached so far, found in that concept's structure, or, for a native concept, in its pinned definition. An operator that handles a value according to its concept MUST handle a variable according to the concept its path reaches, never the root's concept: PipeLLM's attachment of images and documents to the model call, PipeImgGen's injection of reference images, and PipeJudge's presentation of images and documents with its evidence apply to the reached concept, whether the path reaches a single value or a list. With page = "Page", @page.page_view reaches the page_view field of the pinned Page definition, an Image, so PipeLLM attaches it as an image, PipeImgGen injects it as a reference image, and a PipeJudge's prompt presents it as an image.

docs.title: Operator: PipeLLM
docs.text:
Generates output by invoking a large language model with a prompt.
