docs.title: HTTP Runner Protocol
docs.text:
The MTHDS Protocol is the minimal HTTP contract every MTHDS runner implements. Any server that serves its five required routes with the shapes defined here is an MTHDS-compliant runner. A runner that keeps a blob store also serves the optional blob routes, and one that keeps a run store also serves the optional run reads and honours idempotency keys. A runner is just a runner: it executes methods, validates bundles, and reports what models it can route to and what version it is. The protocol requires no run store of it, and it owns no user, billing, or catalog concepts.

The normative artifact is the OpenAPI document: mthds-protocol.openapi.yaml. This page walks through it in prose, then renders it route by route — every parameter, request body, and response schema — in the route reference below. Where prose and YAML disagree, the YAML wins.

docs.title: The routes
docs.text:
Method Path Purpose POST /execute Execute a method synchronously; the full output comes back in the response. POST /start Start a method asynchronously; returns its pipeline_run_id immediately (202). Completion delivery is implementation-defined. POST /validate Parse, validate, and dry-run an MTHDS bundle. GET /models The models this runner can route to. Optional ?type= filter on the model category (llm · extract · img_gen · search · judgment). GET /version Always public. Protocol and runner versions — the handshake clients use for feature detection. POST /blobs/missing Optional, served by a runner that keeps a blob store. Which of the listed blobs the runner lacks, and where to upload each. PUT /blobs/{sha256} Optional. Uploads one blob's bytes to a runner that stores them itself. GET /runs/{pipeline_run_id}/status Optional, served by a runner that keeps a run store. A run's status, and its problem once it has failed. GET /runs/{pipeline_run_id}/results Optional. A completed run's output, as /execute answers it.

The first five routes are required of every runner. The blob routes are served by a runner whose /version declares blob_store: true, and PUT /blobs/{sha256} only by one that stores uploaded bytes itself rather than pointing its senders at another upload target. The run reads are served by a runner whose /version declares run_store: true, which also honours an Idempotency-Key header on /execute and /start.

Every error is a problem document of RFC 9457, served as application/problem+json, that carries the MTHDS core members described under Errors. Auth is implementation-defined: a bearer-token slot is reserved, and anonymous access is allowed for self-hosted runners.

docs.title: Base URL and versioning
docs.text:
Protocol paths are version-agnostic. The version segment belongs to the server base URL, chosen by the implementation:

http://localhost:8081/v1/execute
https://api.example.com/v1/execute

The protocol itself is versioned by this standard (protocol_version in /version), on its own cadence and independently of the standard version; each implementation versions its own mount point. A client written against the protocol composes {base_url}/{path} and never inspects the base URL's structure.

docs.title: Executing a method
docs.text:
POST /execute is blocking: the response carries the method's full output. The request body is a RunRequest:

{
  "pipe_code": "analyze_contract",
  "files": {
    "METHODS.toml": "[package]\nname = \"contract_review\"\n...",
    "contracts.mthds": "domain = \"legal\"\n...",
    "templates/report.html": "<html>...",
    "templates/logo.png": { "base64": "iVBORw0KGgo..." }
  },
  "inputs": {
    "contract": { "concept": "native.Document", "content": { "url": "..." } }
  }
}

files carries the method: its whole method tree, as a map from tree path to file entry (see Method files below). At least one of pipe_code / files is required, and pipe_code alone names a pipe the runner already holds. When files is given without pipe_code, the run starts at the manifest's main_pipe when the tree holds a METHODS.toml at its root, or else, in a method with no manifest, at the one main_pipe its bundles declare. A tree whose manifest declares no main_pipe, or with no manifest whose bundles declare none or several, is refused with a 422 naming its bundles by their tree paths. Optional fields: output_name, output_multiplicity, dynamic_output_concept_ref. Each input is a stuff in the wire form the CLI I/O Contract defines: concept names the concept by its crate key, as a string, and content is its value.

The 200 response is a RunResultExecute — the completed run, holding two base fields: pipeline_run_id (mandatory, server-generated and authoritative) and pipe_output (the method's serialized output; always present — a completed run has output, either a value or an explicit absence document). Anything more an implementation returns — a run state, timestamps, output naming, anything else — is an extension field (see Extension policy), declared and documented by that implementation.

pipe_output is a working memory of stuffs in the same wire form as the inputs, and it carries references only: a concept's definition never travels in a working memory. A client that needs the structure behind a concept resolves the key against the library crate, or reads it from the pipe_io_contracts a validating runner reports. The stuff's shape is the standard's, not the protocol's: the OpenAPI document types an input's concept as a string and leaves pipe_output an open object, the CLI I/O Contract fixes what its entries look like, and a change to that shape moves the standard version and no protocol number — the way the recommended extension fields of the validate report are shaped by their own pages.

The protocol sets no time limit on /execute; deployments cap it at their proxy layer. For long-running methods prefer /start. Implementations MAY answer 202 + RunResultStart (just the run id, no output yet) with a Location header pointing at an implementation-defined status resource when they cannot hold the connection open (RFC 9110 asynchronous pattern). A runner that keeps a run store points it at the run's status read and keeps the run's output for its results read. Simple runners never emit 202; clients that cannot handle it should use /start.

docs.title: Method files
docs.text:
A request's files map holds every file of the method's tree under its tree path: its bundles, its manifest when it has one, and every other file a step may read or that travels with the method, such as a Python module, a template, an image or a requirements.txt. Each value is a file entry in one of three forms:

  • a string, the file's text, whose bytes are its UTF-8 encoding;
  • { "base64": "…" }, any bytes, in standard padded Base64, canonical, with its pad bits zero;
  • { "sha256": "…", "size": … }, bytes the runner already holds in its blob store, named by their SHA-256 in lowercase hexadecimal and their length, a JSON integer written without a fraction or an exponent.

The map must form a tree. A runner refuses with a 422 naming the offending path a map in which:

  • a key is not a tree path, such as a key not already in NFC, which a runner refuses rather than normalize, or names a file the membership rule could never admit, such as a dotfile or a run's inputs file, named inputs.json or inputs.toml at any depth;
  • one path is given twice, as written or once its JSON escapes are decoded, or an entry object gives one of its own keys twice;
  • two paths collide, or one collides with a directory of another, under the Unicode full case folding the method tree defines, such as readme.md beside README.md, STRASSE.txt beside straße.txt, or Templates beside templates/letter.html;
  • an entry is malformed, such as Base64 whose pad bits are not zero, or a size written 13.0.

A hash entry resolves only in the runner's own blob store, and only when the runner holds those bytes at the stated size. A runner without a blob store, or one that does not hold every hash a request names, answers with a 422 problem coded request.blobs_missing, whose params.missing_blobs lists, in lowercase hexadecimal, each hash it does not hold, so a sender learns in one answer which files to supply:

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/request.blobs_missing",
  "title": "The runner does not hold some files sent by hash",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "This runner does not hold a file the request sends by hash.",
  "code": "request.blobs_missing",
  "domain": "input",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "change_input",
    "detail": "Upload each listed blob, or send its file inline if this runner keeps no blob store, then send the request again."
  },
  "params": {
    "missing_blobs": ["3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0"]
  }
}

Supplying the listed files and sending the request again is a change to the request, so the step is change_input. A sender uploads each listed blob to a runner that keeps a blob store, as Sending files by hash describes, and sends each listed file inline to a runner whose GET /version does not declare blob_store: true, since such a runner serves no upload route. The tree's files are the method's own: a file a caller supplies for one run is an input, never an entry of files.

A runner reads a method only from the files it is sent. A file reference resolves in the tree's set of paths and a hash in the blob store, so no request names a path on the runner's own disk. Each implementation bounds a file's size, the tree's file count and its total size, and the total of the inline entries, and refuses a tree past one of them with a problem naming the limit.

docs.title: Starting a method asynchronously
docs.text:
POST /start accepts the same RunRequest body as /execute — the protocol declares no start-only request fields. Anything an implementation accepts on top (a client-supplied run identifier, anything else) is an extension arg (see Extension policy), defined and documented by that implementation.

The response is 202 + RunResultStart — just the authoritative server-generated pipeline_run_id (plus any implementation extension fields). A started run has no output yet.

docs.title: No run store, no completion channel
docs.text: The protocol mandates no run store, and it defines no completion channel for /start: nothing tells a caller that an asynchronous run has finished, and a channel that does, such as a webhook, is implementation-defined and outside the protocol (see Extension policy). A bare runner is not required to answer "what happened to run X?" after the fact. A runner that keeps a run store answers it through the optional run reads, which a caller polls, and declares so with run_store: true in GET /version. A client that must work against every runner relies on /execute's response, and relies on /start only once GET /version has declared a run store or the implementation documents a channel of its own.

docs.title: Validating a bundle
docs.text:
POST /validate takes files, the method's tree as /execute takes it (see Method files), and an optional allow_signatures flag (default false — strict; when true, the validation sweep tolerates unimplemented pipe signatures by minting a mock). A validating runner judges the whole tree: every bundle, and every file a bundle names by file reference or by a PipeFunc's import path.

/validate is a diagnostic endpoint: its job is to return a verdict about the submitted bundle, and every verdict it can produce — valid or invalid — rides a 200, discriminated in the body on the mandatory is_valid field.

  • is_valid: true — the bundle is valid. The protocol declares the is_valid discriminant plus the runnability facts (is_runnable, and pending_signatures — refs of pipes still declared as unimplemented signatures); implementations MAY include their own artifacts (parsed structures, graphs, anything else) as additional properties.
  • is_valid: false — the bundle is invalid. The body carries errors[], a non-empty list of problem items, one per fault, each with its own code, detail, params and location and optionally suggestions and a suggested_fix, plus is_runnable: false and an optional message. The structural artifacts of a valid report are absent.

Either arm may carry warnings[]: advisory findings in the same item schema, which never make a bundle invalid. On every arm a member with no value is left out rather than written as null, in the items of warnings as in those of errors. An item carries no verdict of its own: is_valid is the verdict, and a reader that needs an item's domain reads it from the item's code.

Three recommended extension fields. The protocol's base fields stay exactly as listed above, but three artifacts are common enough — and useful enough to a client that has just learned a bundle is valid — that the standard names them and fixes their shapes rather than letting each implementation invent its own. On the is_valid: true arm, an implementation SHOULD report them under these names: pipe_io_contracts, the per-pipe input and output contracts, whose shape is defined by Pipe I/O Contracts; input_form, the per-pipe ordered presentation view of a method's inputs, whose shape is defined by Input-Form Descriptor; and output_form, the per-pipe presentation view of what each pipe resolves to, whose shape is defined by Output-Form Descriptor. All three derive from the validated library, so none can appear on the is_valid: false arm — there is no library to derive from when loading or wiring failed. They remain extension fields in the sense of the extension policy: a conformant runner may omit them, and a client written against the base fields alone is unaffected. What the standard fixes is that a runner reporting them reports these shapes under these names. How a caller asks for them — always on, an opt-in request token, a separate route — is implementation-defined; all three artifacts are equally derivable offline from a resolved library, and the protocol carriage is one way to obtain them, not what they are.

A client pattern-matches is_valid to learn the verdict — it never inspects a status code or catches an exception body. Non-2xx is reserved for the cases where no verdict could be produced: a malformed request body is a 422 problem, auth a 401/403, a server fault a 5xx. So a non-2xx on /validate always means "the endpoint could not produce a verdict," never "your bundle is bad" — which keeps expected validation failures out of the 4xx error budget and never editorializes a verdict into a spurious retry. Signatures are never an error: an unimplemented signature reached during validation is a runnability fact (is_runnable: false + pending_signatures), not a validation failure, and allow_signatures only affects the dry-run sweep, not the verdict.

docs.title: Sending files by hash
docs.text:
A runner MAY keep a blob store: bytes keyed by their SHA-256, written once and never changed. A runner that keeps one declares blob_store: true in GET /version and serves POST /blobs/missing, so a sender uploads each file at most once and then sends the method's tree by hash. A second run of an unchanged method uploads nothing, and editing one template uploads one file.

  1. The sender lists the method's tree and computes each file's SHA-256 and the tree digest.
  2. It asks POST /blobs/missing which of those blobs the runner lacks.
  3. It uploads each missing blob as the answer says.
  4. It sends the run, or the validation, with a hash entry for each file it chose to send by hash.

A sender chooses per file between an inline entry and a hash entry, and may mix both in one request; neither form is second-class.

docs.title: POST /blobs/missing
docs.text:
The request lists blobs by hash and size, each size a JSON integer written without a fraction or an exponent, as in a hash entry, and may name the tree they make up:

{
  "digest": "sha256:801fca61b41566e46d3fb1923e323590da7a539fd3e7af7455e7cba3934d4674",
  "blobs": [
    { "sha256": "af12591480ada38cf107d1a76bc5e2e111ad4c7ec5f3a2a63d058f5f5ab6b91c", "size": 12 },
    { "sha256": "3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0", "size": 13 }
  ]
}

The 200 answer lists every blob of the request the runner does not hold, each with its size, a JSON integer written in the same way, and where to upload it:

{
  "missing": [
    {
      "sha256": "3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0",
      "size": 13,
      "upload": {
        "method": "PUT",
        "url": "https://runner.example.com/v1/blobs/3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0",
        "headers": { "content-type": "application/octet-stream" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

To upload a missing blob, the sender sends the blob's bytes as the whole body of a request with the given method to the given url, carrying exactly the given headers. The upload target is the runner's to choose: its own PUT /blobs/{sha256}, or any other address that stores the bytes where the runner reads its blobs. A blob the runner holds is left out of missing, and an empty missing means the sender has nothing to upload.

The optional digest names the tree the listed blobs make up. A runner that keeps a record of the trees it has held in full MAY answer with an empty missing when it holds the tree that digest names, which makes the check for an unchanged method one lookup however many files it has. It records a tree only after checking that it holds every file the tree's listing names, and never takes an uploaded blob as such a record, since anyone can upload bytes that happen to form a listing.

A request naming one hash twice with different sizes is a 422, and so is a blob past the runner's limits, refused before anything is uploaded with a problem naming the limit. Which callers share a blob store is the runner's policy: a hash entry resolves only in the store the runner keeps for its caller, and a runner serving several tenants SHOULD keep each one's blobs apart, so that holding a hash never tells one tenant what another has stored.

docs.title: PUT /blobs/{sha256}
docs.text: The upload target of a runner that stores bytes itself. The body is the blob's bytes and nothing else. The runner computes their SHA-256 and refuses with a 422 a body whose hash differs from the one in the path. A blob is written once and never changed, so uploading bytes the runner already holds succeeds without changing anything; either way the answer is a 204.

docs.title: Reading a run and idempotency keys
docs.text:
A runner MAY keep a run store: a record of the runs it has started, kept by their pipeline_run_id. A runner that keeps one declares run_store: true in GET /version, serves the two run reads below, and honours an idempotency key on /execute and /start. A runner that declares no run store serves neither read and ignores the key. Like the blob routes, this section is optional: the protocol requires no run store, and a runner without one is conformant.

A caller starts a run under an idempotency key of its choosing:

POST /start
Idempotency-Key: 0b6e3c0e-5d0a-4f3e-8a57-9a1f4c2d7e11
Content-Type: application/json

{ "pipe_code": "analyze_contract", "files": { "contracts.mthds": "domain = \"legal\"\n..." }, "inputs": { "contract": { "concept": "native.Document", "content": { "url": "..." } } } }

If the 202 answer is lost, the caller sends the same request again under the same key within 24 hours of the first, the least time a runner keeps a key, and the runner answers with the run the first request started rather than starting a second one. The caller then polls the run's status and reads its output once it has completed:

GET /runs/8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10/status
GET /runs/8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10/results

docs.title: The run store
docs.text:
A runner that keeps a run store records every run it starts, through /execute and /start alike, under the pipeline_run_id it answered with, together with the run's status and, once the run has failed, its problem. It keeps the output of every completed run whose output did not travel in an answer, that is a run started by /start and one that /execute answered with a 202, so that the results read can serve it. It may also keep the output of a run whose /execute answer carried it. How long it keeps a run is its own policy, and a run it no longer holds reads as one it never held.

A run is read by the caller that started it, or by whoever else the runner's policy lets read it. A runner answers an id naming a run the caller may not read exactly as it answers an id naming no run, so that an id never tells a caller about a run it cannot read.

docs.title: GET /runs/{pipeline_run_id}/status
docs.text:
The status read answers 200 with the run's pipeline_run_id, its status, and its error once it has failed:

{
  "pipeline_run_id": "8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10",
  "status": "failed",
  "error": {
    "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/pipe.output_multiplicity",
    "title": "A pipe's output does not have the declared multiplicity",
    "detail": "Pipe 'extract_clauses' produced a list, but its output 'clause' is declared as a single item.",
    "code": "pipe.output_multiplicity",
    "domain": "method",
    "retry": "no",
    "next_step": {
      "kind": "change_method",
      "detail": "Declare the output 'clause' as a list, or make pipe 'extract_clauses' produce a single item."
    },
    "params": { "pipe": "extract_clauses", "output": "clause", "declared": "single", "produced": "list" },
    "location": { "pipe": "extract_clauses", "path": ["review_contract", "extract_clauses"] },
    "pipeline_run_id": "8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10"
  }
}

A run's status is one of:

Status Ended Meaning pending no The runner accepted the run and has not begun executing it. running no The run is executing. completed yes The run ended with its output, which the results read serves. failed yes The run ended without output. error holds its problem, whose code says why, such as run.cancelled for a run its caller cancelled or run.timed_out for one that passed its time limit.

error is the run's own problem, as the run's record keeps it: a problem document without status, since it is not the body of a response. It is present exactly when status is failed. The status read does not fail because the run failed: its 200 answers a question about the run, and the run's problem rides inside it. A runner that can no longer learn how a run ended, such as when whatever executed it vanished without reporting, ends it failed with the problem run.lost, whose retry is yes, since a new run may succeed.

A run ends completed or failed, and the statuses of a run that has ended are closed: a later protocol version may add a status only for a run that has not ended. So a runner MUST NOT emit a status this page does not list, and a client that meets a status it does not know reads the run as not ended and reads it again later. A runner may set a Retry-After header on the 200 of a run that has not ended, to say when to read it again.

docs.title: GET /runs/{pipeline_run_id}/results
docs.text:
The results read answers a completed run with a 200 whose body is the one /execute answers with, a RunResultExecute holding the run's pipeline_run_id and its pipe_output, so a client that started a run with /start reads the same output it would have read from /execute. Any other run is answered with a problem: run.not_finished before the run has ended, run.failed once it has ended without output, and run.results_not_stored for a completed run whose output travelled in /execute's answer and was not kept. A read of a failed run's results carries the run's own problem as its run_error member, beside the read's own code:

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/run.failed",
  "title": "The run did not succeed",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Run '8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10' ended without output, so it has no results.",
  "code": "run.failed",
  "domain": "runtime",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "read_run",
    "detail": "Read the run's own problem in run_error to learn why it failed."
  },
  "params": { "pipeline_run_id": "8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10", "run_status": "failed" },
  "pipeline_run_id": "8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10",
  "run_error": {
    "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/run.timed_out",
    "title": "The run passed its time limit",
    "detail": "The run did not end within this runner's run time limit.",
    "code": "run.timed_out",
    "domain": "method",
    "retry": "no",
    "next_step": { "kind": "change_method", "detail": "Make the method do less work in one run." },
    "params": { "timeout": 3600 },
    "pipeline_run_id": "8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10"
  }
}

A problem about a run is not the problem of the read that returned it. Reading the results again changes nothing, so the read's retry is no, and the run's own problem, in run_error, says who must act and whether a new run may succeed.

docs.title: Idempotency keys
docs.text:
A client sending /execute or /start may name the request with an Idempotency-Key header: a string of 1 to 255 visible ASCII characters, from ! to ~, that the client chooses and never uses for another request, such as a UUID. A runner that declares run_store: true then runs the request at most once while it holds the key: a repeat of it under the same key, from the same caller, is answered from that one execution. A client whose answer was lost, or whose request may or may not have reached the runner, sends the request again under its key within the period below and learns the outcome without starting a second run. A client SHOULD send a key on every request that starts a run, since only a request that carried one can be repeated safely. A runner that honours keys refuses a key outside that form with a 422 coded request.invalid.

A runner keeps each key per caller, so that two callers' keys never meet, and for at least 24 hours after the first request under it, with what it needs to answer a repeat: a fingerprint of the request, the run the request started, and the answer it gave when it keeps that answer. A request under a key the runner no longer holds is a first request. So every promise this section makes about a repeat holds within that period: a repeat that reaches the runner within 24 hours of the first request under its key is answered as described below, and past them the protocol promises nothing, since a runner that has let the key go takes the repeat as a first request and may start a second run. A client that cannot repeat a request within the period does not repeat it to learn its outcome: it reads the run when it knows the run's pipeline_run_id, and otherwise treats the outcome as unknown and never repeats the request automatically.

A repeat is the same request when it goes to the same route with a body of the same JSON value, whatever the order of its members and its whitespace. A request under a held key that is not the same request is refused with request.idempotency_conflict, whether the first request is still running or has ended: a key names one request, and a different request takes a new key. The same request under a held key is answered as follows:

  • While the first request is still being handled and has started no run, with request.idempotency_key_in_use, carrying retry_after when the runner knows how long to wait. The client sends the same request again, unchanged, after waiting.
  • On /start, once the first request has started its run, with the first answer, a 202 + RunResultStart naming that run. Nothing starts again.
  • On /execute, once the first request has started its run, with the first answer when the runner can give it again from what it kept of the answer or of the run: the same 200 and output, or the same problem. While the run has not ended, the runner answers with a 202 + RunResultStart naming the run, with a Location header pointing at its status read, the asynchronous answer /execute may already give. Once the run has ended and the runner kept neither its answer nor its output, it answers with run.answer_not_kept, and the client reads the run's status to learn how it ended.
  • When the first request was refused before it started a run, as a first request: a refusal takes no effect, so it leaves the key free.

The key changes nothing else about a request. A run's id is still the runner's, and a request without a key is never deduplicated. A runner that honours the key on a route of its own, beyond /execute and /start, answers a repeat whose answer it never gives twice, such as one that hands out a secret, with request.already_executed, and the client reads what the first request created rather than sending it again. A runner that keeps no run store ignores the header, so that a repeat under the key would start a second run: a client repeats a request under its key only against a runner whose GET /version declares run_store: true.

This is what the next step of a problem whose retry is outcome_unknown rests on. Against a runner that keeps a run store, the client learns the outcome by reading the run whose pipeline_run_id the problem carries or, when no answer named the run, by sending the request again under the same idempotency key within 24 hours of the first request under it, which answers with the run the first request started and never starts a second. Past that period a repeat may start a second run, so a client that knows no run to read leaves the outcome unknown.

The protocol defines no route that changes a run. A runner that offers one, such as a route that cancels a run, answers a change asked of a run that has already ended with run.already_ended.

docs.title: The codes of the run reads and idempotency keys
docs.text:
Every code in the table below is a core code that the run reads and idempotency keys introduce. Each code's title, parameters and documentation are the core registry's, and each code in the table declares the same step for its actor and for any other reader. The other codes this section names, such as request.invalid, run.cancelled and run.timed_out, are core codes it does not introduce, whose values are the core registry's.

Code Answered Status Domain Retry Step run.not_found By either read, when the id names no run the caller can read. 404 input no change_input run.not_finished By the results read, before the run has ended, with retry_after when known. 409 runtime yes wait run.failed By the results read, once the run has ended without output, with the run's problem in run_error. 409 runtime no read_run run.results_not_stored By the results read, for a completed run whose output travelled in /execute's answer and was not kept. 404 input no read_run run.lost As a failed run's own problem, when the runner can no longer learn how the run ended. Its status is the one /execute answers it with. 500 runtime yes retry run.answer_not_kept By /execute, to the same request under a held key, once the run has ended and the runner kept neither its answer nor its output. 409 input no read_run run.already_ended By a runner's own route that changes a run, such as a cancellation, once the run has ended. 409 input no read_run request.idempotency_conflict To a request under a held key that is not the same request. 409 input no change_input request.idempotency_key_in_use To the same request under a held key, while the first request is still being handled and has started no run, with retry_after when known. 409 runtime yes wait request.already_executed To a repeat under a held key, on a runner's own route whose answer is never given twice. 409 input no read_run

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
GET /models returns the runner's model deck — the models it can route to ({name, type} entries), optionally filtered by category. Implementations may add their own routing metadata (aliases, fallback chains, anything else) as additional properties.

GET /version is always public (no auth). It returns protocol_version (required), an optional runner_version, an optional blob_store flag, which is true for a runner that keeps a blob store and serves the blob routes, and false or absent for one that does not, and an optional run_store flag, which is true for a runner that keeps a run store, serves the run reads and honours idempotency keys, and false or absent for one that does not — implementations may add their own identification on top:

{
  "protocol_version": "2.0.0",
  "runner_version": "2.3.0",
  "blob_store": true,
  "run_store": true
}

Clients use /version as the handshake: it reports the protocol and runner versions, whether the runner takes files by hash and whether it can be asked about a run after the fact, and any additional properties let clients detect vendor extensions before relying on them.

docs.title: Model categories
docs.text:
A deck entry's type is its model category. A category is a settings family of the language: it names the inline settings structure a model serves, and so the pipes whose model field can name that model.

Category Settings family Pipes that name a model of it llm LLMSetting PipeLLM, PipeStructure extract ExtractSetting PipeExtract img_gen ImgGenSetting PipeImgGen search SearchSetting PipeSearch judgment JudgmentSetting PipeJudge

The category follows the settings family, not the operator: PipeStructure takes LLMSetting, so its models are listed under llm. When the standard adds a settings family, the protocol adds its category in its next minor version.

The two sides of the wire carry different obligations:

  • A runner emits only the protocol's categories. A runner MUST NOT put a value the protocol does not define in a deck entry's type, and MUST NOT accept one on the ?type= filter, which answers it with a 422. A model of a family the protocol does not define — a vendor's own operator — is reported, if at all, under an extension property of the runner's choosing, never under an invented category and never as an entry of models without one.
  • A client accepts any category. A client reading a model list MUST NOT fail it because an entry carries a category it does not recognize; it keeps that entry with its raw value or leaves it out.

The enum on a deck entry's type in the OpenAPI document is the emitter's contract, the set a runner may report. A client that derives its types or its validation from that document widens the field to any string, as the reader rule requires.

The reader rule is what makes a new category a minor change: a client written against one protocol version keeps working when a runner of a later minor version reports a category the client has never heard of. It governs a client reading a list on purpose. A tool that checks a runner, such as a conformance harness, is checking the emitter rule and stays free to reject an unknown value. In the other direction, a client that filters on a category its runner's protocol version does not define gets a 422, and learns from GET /version which protocol version the runner implements.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error a runner answers is a problem document of RFC 9457, served as application/problem+json, carrying the MTHDS core members beside the RFC's own. A run that failed, as the caller of /execute reads it:

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/pipe.output_multiplicity",
  "title": "A pipe's output does not have the declared multiplicity",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Pipe 'extract_clauses' produced a list, but its output 'clause' is declared as a single item.",
  "code": "pipe.output_multiplicity",
  "domain": "method",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "change_method",
    "detail": "Declare the output 'clause' as a list, or make pipe 'extract_clauses' produce a single item."
  },
  "params": { "pipe": "extract_clauses", "output": "clause", "declared": "single", "produced": "list" },
  "location": { "pipe": "extract_clauses", "path": ["review_contract", "extract_clauses"] },
  "pipeline_run_id": "8c1f6a52-3d1e-4b7a-9f0e-2a5c7d9e4b10"
}

The first four members are the RFC's, and the rest are the MTHDS core's:

Member Present Meaning type always The code's documentation page, derived from the code (see The type URI). title always The code's short title, the same for every occurrence of the code. status on an HTTP response The HTTP status of the response the problem is the body of. A runner sets it on every response; a problem kept elsewhere, such as in a run's record, leaves it out. detail always This occurrence, in one or two sentences a person can read. code always The registry code: what happened. domain always Who must act. retry always Whether repeating the operation that produced the problem can succeed. retry_after when known Seconds to wait before repeating it, beside a retry of yes. next_step always What the reader should do next: a kind from a closed list and a detail sentence. params when the code declares parameters The typed facts the problem's sentences were written from. location when the error has a place Where in the method, the request or the run. errors when the problem has several faults One item per fault. pipeline_run_id when a run exists The run the error belongs to, as /execute and /start name it. run_error on a read of a failed run's results The run's own problem, nested, as the results read describes.

The RFC's optional instance member is not part of the core: a runner may send it, and a client written against the protocol does not read it.

The code decides. Every problem carries exactly one code from a registry, and its domain, its retry verdict, its next step, its title and its HTTP status are properties of that code. The wire carries them so that a reader needs no lookup, but a runner never sets them independently of the code: two cases that need different verdicts are two codes. A client branches on code, and on domain, retry and next_step.kind when it handles several codes alike. It never parses title, detail or next_step.detail, which are written for a person, so every fact they state is also a member: the typed facts in params, the place in location. No member of a problem carries the content of a run's inputs or outputs.

docs.title: Codes
docs.text:
A code is lowercase and dotted, each segment matching [a-z][a-z0-9_]*. A core code is bare, exactly a family and a name, such as input.missing or request.blobs_missing. A code belongs to the core when any conforming runner or client could raise it, independently of hosting, billing or a vendor's components. The MTHDS core registry lists the core codes and gives each its title, domain, retry verdict, steps, parameters and HTTP status. A code's family is the code without its last segment, so request.blobs_missing belongs to the family request.

Extension codes. Every other code starts with a prefix its owner registers, followed by a family and a name: <prefix>.<family>.<name>, such as acme.billing.credit_exhausted. A prefix is one segment of the same form, it is never the name of a core family, and it belongs to one owner, who alone adds codes under it. What the protocol leaves to implementations, such as billing or a catalog of saved methods, is coded under the implementation's own prefix.

Declaring a prefix. An owner declares an extension prefix in two steps:

  1. It publishes a registry of its own codes, in the format of the core registry, that names the prefix and the base URL its codes' pages are published under, and declares for each code everything the core registry declares for a core code.
  2. It registers the prefix with the standard, through the contribution process, as an entry of the core registry's list of extension prefixes naming the prefix, its owner and that base URL. A registered prefix is never reassigned to another owner.

A runner emits a code under a prefix only once the prefix is registered and the code is in its owner's registry.

docs.title: The type URI
docs.text: type is derived from the code and its owner's base URL: the base URL, a slash, then the whole code. The core's base URL is https://mthds.ai/errors, so the core code input.missing has the type https://mthds.ai/errors/input.missing. An extension code is joined, its prefix included, to the base URL its prefix is registered with: under a prefix registered with https://errors.acme.example, the code acme.billing.credit_exhausted has the type https://errors.acme.example/acme.billing.credit_exhausted. The page at a type URI says what the code means and what to do about it, and the Error Codes page lists every core code's. Because type and code name the same thing one to one, a client branches on code and never takes a code apart from type.

docs.title: Domain: who must act
docs.text:
The domain answers the first question a reader has: can I fix this myself, and if not, who can. Its list is closed:

Domain Who acts Examples input The caller, by changing the request or its inputs A required input is missing; an input is not the declared concept; a request body is malformed; the runner does not hold a file sent by hash. method The method's author, by changing the method The method does not validate; a pipe's output has the wrong multiplicity at run time; the method names a model that exists nowhere. account The account's owner A refused credential; a missing permission; an exhausted quota. operator Whoever runs the runtime The method names a model that exists, but this runner serves no backend for it; a misconfigured server. runtime Nobody beforehand: wait, retry or report A provider outage; a timeout; a model's structured output that did not match its schema; a fault of the runtime itself.

A case whose actor depends on where something came from is two codes: a URL the runner refuses to fetch is the caller's when an input named it and the method's author's when the method did.

docs.title: Retry
docs.text:
retry says whether repeating the operation that produced the problem can succeed, and its list is closed:

  • no: repeating it fails the same way.
  • yes: repeating it may succeed, after retry_after seconds when that member is given.
  • outcome_unknown: the operation may already have taken effect, such as a request whose connection dropped after the runner received it. A client never repeats such an operation automatically; it follows the next step to learn the outcome first. Against a runner that keeps a run store, that step reads the run, or sends the request again under the same idempotency key within 24 hours of the first request under it, which then never runs it twice (Idempotency keys). Past those 24 hours a repeat may start a second run, so a client that knows no run to read leaves the outcome unknown.

On a run's own problem the operation is the run, so yes means that a new run with the same inputs may succeed.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
next_step tells the reader what to do next, as a kind from a closed list and a detail sentence:

Kind What the reader does retry Repeats the operation. wait Waits, then checks again later. read_run Reads the run to learn its outcome, such as through the status read of a runner that keeps a run store. refresh Fetches the latest state, such as a fresh credential, and applies the change again. change_input Changes the request or its inputs, which includes supplying the files a runner lacks, by uploading them or by sending them inline, and sending the request again. change_method Changes the method. change_model Chooses another model. check_credentials Checks the credential the request sent. request_access Asks for the permission the operation needs. check_account Checks the account's credit, plan or quotas. fix_configuration Fixes the runtime's configuration. upgrade Upgrades the client or the runtime. contact_owner Contacts the owner of the method or of the account. report Reports the problem, with the identifiers it carries.

A step is aimed at whoever reads the problem, not at the domain's actor. Each code declares a step for its actor and one for any other reader: a caller who runs a method someone else owns reads contact_owner where the method's author would read change_method, and a member of an account who cannot change it reads contact_owner where its owner would read check_account. There is no unknown step: every code declares its steps, and the catch-all code, for a fault no other code describes, says report.

docs.title: Parameters and location
docs.text:
params holds the typed facts the problem's sentences were written from, such as the pipe, the output and the two multiplicities in the example above, so that a client acts on data rather than on prose. Each code declares its parameters and their types in its registry, and params is present when the code declares any. A parameter holds an identifier, a number or an enumerated value, or, where its code declares so, the caller's own text, such as a parser's finding about the caller's method; it never holds the content of a run's inputs or outputs.

location says where the error happened. Every member is optional:

Member Meaning pipe The failing pipe's code. path The pipe codes from the run's main pipe down to the failing one. input The name of the input the error concerns. field A dotted path inside an input or a request body. item The index of the batch item that failed, counted from 0. attempt The attempt that failed, counted from 1. file The tree path of the method's file the error is in. line The line in file, counted from 1. column The column in line, counted from 1.

The location of a run's problem is its root fault's, so it names the pipe that failed rather than the controller around it.

docs.title: Itemized errors
docs.text:
A problem with several faults, such as a method that does not validate, carries one item per fault in errors, and the errors and warnings of a validate verdict are items of the same schema:

{
  "code": "method.input_unused",
  "detail": "Pipe 'summarize' declares the input 'draft' but never reads it.",
  "params": { "pipe": "summarize", "variables": ["draft"] },
  "location": { "pipe": "summarize", "file": "contracts.mthds", "line": 12, "column": 1 },
  "suggested_fix": {
    "fix_code": "remove-unused-input",
    "description": "Remove the input 'draft' from pipe 'summarize'.",
    "safety": "unsafe",
    "ops": [
      { "kind": "delete_key", "table_path": ["pipe", "summarize", "inputs"], "key": "draft" }
    ]
  }
}
Member Present Meaning code always The fault's code. detail always This fault, in one or two sentences a person can read. params when the code declares parameters The fault's typed facts. location when the fault has a place Where the fault is. suggestions optional The names a near miss most likely meant, the likeliest first. suggested_fix optional A semantic patch that fixes the fault.

An item carries no verdict of its own: the problem or the verdict that holds it does, and a reader that needs an item's domain reads it from the item's code.

docs.title: Suggested fixes
docs.text:
A suggested_fix is a semantic patch over a bundle: a list of operations addressed by TOML key path, never a text diff. Its members are fix_code, the implementation's kebab-case name for the rule that produced it; description, one sentence saying what it does; safety; file, the tree path of the bundle it patches, which defaults to the file the item's location names; and ops, a non-empty list of operations discriminated on kind.

safety is safe for a fix that may be applied without asking anyone, and unsafe for a likely correction that a person or an agent confirms before it is applied.

Every operation names a table by table_path, the table's key path from the document root, each segment one key as written, and empty for the root table:

Kind Members Effect set_key table_path, key, value Writes key = value in the table, creating the key when the table does not hold it and replacing a scalar or array value it holds; when the key holds a table, the operation is a conflict and changes nothing. The value is a TOML scalar or an inline table of scalars. ensure_table table_path Creates the table at table_path when it is absent and the table above it exists, and leaves an existing one untouched. delete_key table_path, key Removes key from the table. delete_table table_path Removes the table at table_path, every part of it included. rename_table_key table_path, key, new_key Renames key to new_key within the table, keeping its value and its position. move_key table_path, key, new_table_path, new_key Moves key, with its whole value, into the table at new_table_path under new_key, creating the destination tables that do not exist. remap_value table_path, key, mapping Rewrites the string value of key through mapping, from an old value to its new one, and does nothing when the value is not a key of the mapping. It rewrites its own target by design, which is never a conflict.

For ensure_table and delete_table, table_path names the table acted on rather than the table holding a key, so it is never empty, and the root table is never removed.

The operations apply in order, each to the document the previous one left. What an operation does with an absent target depends on its kind. A deletion, a rename, a move or a remap whose target is absent, such as a key to delete or the table holding it, is skipped. ensure_table creates its table when it is absent, and set_key creates its key when the table does not hold it. Each needs the table that would hold its target: a set_key whose table is absent, or an ensure_table whose parent table is absent, is skipped, so a fix that writes into a table that may be missing puts an ensure_table before the operations that need it, one for each level that may be missing, the outermost first. An operation already in the state it would produce, such as an ensure_table whose table exists or a set_key whose key already holds its value, is skipped too. One that could only proceed by overwriting a key or a table other than its own target, such as a rename or a move onto a key its destination table already holds, is a conflict and changes nothing. Rewriting its own target is no conflict: set_key replaces a scalar or array value its key holds, and remap_value rewrites its value by design. A set_key whose key holds a table is a conflict all the same, and so is an ensure_table whose table_path names a value other than a table; neither changes anything. An applier reports skips and conflicts rather than forcing the change. The operations are the contract, and any diff an applier shows from them is presentation.

docs.title: Readers and emitters
docs.text:
The problem document is closed for emitters and open for readers:

  • A runner emits only what is registered. Every code it emits is in a registry, the core's or that of a registered prefix, and every value it puts in domain, retry, next_step.kind, a fix's safety or an operation's kind is one this page lists. The enums of the OpenAPI document are the emitter's contract.
  • A reader accepts what it does not know. Every schema of the problem document, its items, locations, steps, fixes and operations included, accepts members it does not declare, and a reader ignores a member it does not know, as RFC 9457 requires. A client that derives its types or its validation from the OpenAPI document widens each of these enums to any string, as it does for model categories. An operation's kind selects a variant of a union rather than a value of an enum, so the OpenAPI document gives FixOp a reader-side catch-all, UnknownFixOp, an object whose kind is a string none of the listed kinds, which no runner emits: an operation of a kind the reader does not know still validates, and so do its fix, its item and the problem or verdict holding them. FixOp is a plain oneOf matched on kind, each listed operation fixing it to one value, with no discriminator object, since a discriminator rejects a value its mapping does not name. Such a client keeps that variant rather than closing the union on the kinds this page lists.
  • A reader falls back on the family. A reader that meets a code, a domain or a step kind it does not know reads it by the code's family, as it reads the codes of that family it knows, and when it knows nothing of the family either, it reads the domain as runtime and the step as report. A retry it does not know reads as no, so that nothing is repeated on a guess. An applier that meets an operation kind it does not know applies none of that fix, and a safety it does not know reads as unsafe.
  • An unset member is absent. A member with no value is left out, never written as null, in a problem, in its items and locations, and in a validate verdict's errors and warnings alike.

Because every problem carries its own domain, verdict and step, a client whose registry lags a runner's still reads a problem with a new code correctly by these rules. An item carries only its code, so that guarantee does not reach an item whose code the client does not know, such as an item of a validate verdict, which no problem holds: the client reads such an item by the code's family, and when it knows nothing of the family either, as runtime and report, which need not be the domain and step its code declares. A tool that checks a runner, such as a conformance harness, checks the emitter rules and stays free to reject an unknown value.

docs.title: Extension policy
docs.text: Implementations may extend the surface — extra routes, extra optional request properties, extra response properties — but must not change the meaning or shape of the protocol routes. Both sides of the wire are extension-open: request bodies accept implementation-defined args, and the protocol's response schemas declare only the base fields (additionalProperties allowed). A client written against the MTHDS Protocol runs unmodified against any compliant runner; a vendor's superset may accept and return more, but never diverges on the surface defined here.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
An implementation claiming conformance states it as: implements MTHDS Protocol v2.0. Conformance means: the five required routes exist with the request/response shapes of mthds-protocol.openapi.yaml, every error is an RFC 9457 problem document carrying the core members, with a registered code, /version is public, a runner that declares blob_store: true serves POST /blobs/missing and resolves hash entries from its blob store, and a runner that declares run_store: true serves both run reads and honours an idempotency key on /execute and /start as Reading a run and idempotency keys describes.

The protocol number moves under its own rule — a new route, a new optional field or a new model category is a minor bump, a changed shape or meaning is a major one — independently of the standard version. The recommended extension fields above are not such an addition: they are shaped by their own specification pages and ride a report that is extension-open by policy, so naming one moves no protocol number. See Versioning.

docs.title: Route reference
docs.text: Everything below is rendered at build time from the normative OpenAPI document — do not edit it by hand; edit mthds-protocol.openapi.yaml.

docs.text: Description URL Example — a self-hosted runner. The version segment belongs to the server base URL; protocol paths are version-agnostic. http://localhost:8081/v1 Example — a hosted, protocol-compliant superset. https://api.example.com/v1

docs.title: POST /execute
docs.text:
Execute a method synchronously and return its full output.

Description

Blocking. The protocol sets no time limit; deployments cap it at their proxy layer. For long-running methods prefer /start. Implementations MAY return 202 + RunResultStart (id only) with a Location header pointing at an implementation-defined status resource when they cannot hold the connection open for the full execution (RFC 9110 asynchronous pattern); clients that cannot handle 202 should use /start instead. A runner whose /version declares run_store true points Location at the run's status read, keeps the run's output for its results read, and honours the Idempotency-Key header: the same request repeated under a held key is answered with the first answer when the runner can give it again, with a 202 naming the run while the run has not ended, and with a 409 coded run.answer_not_kept once it has ended and the runner kept neither its answer nor its output.

Input parameters

Parameter In Type Default Nullable Description bearer header string N/A No Token semantics are implementation-defined. Idempotency-Key header string No Names the request, so that a runner whose /version declares run_store true runs it at most once while it holds the key: a string of visible ASCII characters the client chooses and never uses for another request, such as a UUID. The runner keeps each key per caller, for at least 24 hours after the first request under it, and takes a request under a key it no longer holds as a first request, so the protocol promises nothing about a repeat past those 24 hours: a client that cannot repeat within them reads the run when it knows its pipeline_run_id, and otherwise treats the outcome as unknown and never repeats automatically. The same request, the same route with a body of the same JSON value whatever the order of its members and its whitespace, repeated under a held key is answered from the first execution: a 409 coded request.idempotency_key_in_use while the first request is still being handled and has started no run, the first answer once it has started its run, and as a first request when the first was refused before it started a run, which leaves the key free. A different request under a held key is a 409 coded request.idempotency_conflict. A key outside this form is a 422 coded request.invalid. A runner that keeps no run store ignores the header, so a client repeats a request under its key only against a runner that declares run_store true.

docs.title: POST /start
docs.text:
Start a method asynchronously; returns its pipeline_run_id immediately.

Description

Asynchronous. Returns 202 + RunResultStart immediately (pipeline_run_id only). The protocol defines no completion channel: a runner whose /version declares run_store true serves the run reads, which a caller polls, and any channel that tells a caller a run has finished (callbacks, anything else) is implementation-defined and outside the protocol. The returned pipeline_run_id is always authoritative (server-generated). A runner that keeps a run store honours the Idempotency-Key header: the same request repeated under a held key is answered with the first 202, naming the run the first request started, and starts nothing.

docs.title: POST /validate
docs.text:
Parse, validate, and dry-run an MTHDS bundle.

Description

Diagnostic endpoint. Every verdict the validator can produce — valid or invalid — rides a 200, discriminated in the body on is_valid. Non-2xx is reserved for the cases where no verdict could be produced (a malformed request body, auth, a server fault), so a 422 here is a request-shape problem, never "the bundle is invalid".

Input parameters

Parameter In Type Default Nullable Description bearer header string N/A No Token semantics are implementation-defined.

Description

OPTIONAL — served by a runner whose /version declares blob_store true. docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
MTHDS carries two version numbers, and they move independently:

Number Governs Current Standard version The language, the native concept set, the method tree, the manifest and lock formats, the library crate format, the namespace rules, the wire form of a stuff, the core error registry 8.0.0 Protocol version The HTTP runner contract — its routes, their request and response shapes, and the problem document every error is 2.0.0

Both are Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 numbers. Everything else that carries a version — a package's own version, a runner's runner_version, an implementation's release number — belongs to that package, runner, or implementation and is governed by whoever publishes it.

docs.title: The Standard Version
docs.text:
The standard version is the version of this specification. The release of the MTHDS specification, the ## [vX.Y.Z] heading in its changelog, and the MTHDS_STANDARD_VERSION constant in every implementation are one number, not three. There is no separate "documentation release number" running alongside it.

It governs everything this specification defines other than the HTTP protocol:

  • The .mthds file format — the language itself: its sections, its keys, its pipe types, its concept structure language.
  • The native concept definitions — the pinned set every implementation materializes.
  • The method tree — which files make up a method, how a file is named and referenced, the tree digest, the file entry, and requirements.txt.
  • The METHODS.toml format and the methods.lock format.
  • The library crate format and the namespace resolution rules.
  • The CLI I/O contract — the wire form of a stuff, and the envelopes a method reads and writes when it is invoked from a command line.
  • The core error registry — the core codes and everything each declares, and the list of registered extension prefixes.

docs.title: What Bumps the Standard Version
docs.text:
• MAJOR — a breaking change to any of the above. A key removed or renamed, a native concept's shape changed, a rule that changes which files make up a method tree or what its digest is, a rule that makes a previously valid bundle, manifest, or lock file invalid, or a previously invalid one valid in a way that changes what an existing document means.
  • MINOR — an additive change. A new native concept, a new pipe type, a new optional key, a new field type: documents valid under the previous version stay valid and keep their meaning.
  • PATCH — a change that is normatively inert. A clarification, a corrected example, a reworded rule that states what was already true, a new guide, a typo fix.

These classes are read over what authors write — bundles, manifests, lock files, crates. A rule that changes what a runtime must emit or accept on the wire while every authored document stays valid and keeps its meaning is a MINOR change: the changelog marks it breaking, because a runtime conforming to the previous version may have to change, and the number says that no document does.

A release that changes nothing normative is a patch of the standard. That is the deliberate cost of one number: the standard version moves on every release of the specification, and a bump on its own is not evidence that anything changed. What changed is in the changelog.

docs.title: The Pinned Native Set Under One Number
docs.text:
Because a patch release moves the standard version without touching the native set, the pinned set is identified by the standard version in which it last changed, not by the current standard version. native-concepts.md names that version.

An implementation implementing standard version V materializes the pinned set of the greatest version less than or equal to V. So an implementation of 2.3.0 uses the set pinned at 2.0.0 until a later version pins a new one, and two implementations of different patch or minor versions still byte-agree on materialized natives — which is what makes crate fingerprints comparable across them.

docs.title: The Core Error Registry
docs.text:
The core error registry declares the standard version it is published with as its own version, and it moves under the classes above. No change to it makes an authored document invalid, so it never moves the major number:

  • MINOR — a new code, family or extension prefix, a new parameter, or a change to what a runtime emits or a client acts on: a code removed or renamed, a parameter removed, or a code's domain, retry verdict, step kind, HTTP status or parameter type changed. Each of the latter is marked breaking in the changelog, because a runtime or a client following the previous registry may have to change.
  • PATCH — a reworded title, template, meaning, what to do or description, or a corrected reference. These are written for a person, and no reader parses them.

docs.title: mthds_version and the Crate Stamp
docs.text:
Two artifacts carry the standard version, and they mean different things:

  • A manifest's mthds_version is a constraint: the versions of the standard the package declares itself compatible with. It is evaluated against the standard version the runtime implements.
  • A library crate's mthds_version is a stamp: the exact standard version the crate was normalized against, recording which pinned native set was used.

Because both are compared against the standard version, the standard version MUST NOT move backwards. A crate stamped with an older version names an older pinned set, which is exactly what the stamp is for; a constraint written against an older version stays satisfiable.

docs.title: The Protocol Version
docs.text: The HTTP runner protocol is versioned separately, on its own cadence, because a client gates on it independently of the language it writes methods in. A runner reports it as protocol_version from GET /version, and it is the info.version of the normative OpenAPI document.

docs.title: What Bumps the Protocol Version
docs.text:
• MAJOR — a changed shape or a changed meaning. A route removed or renamed, a request or response field removed, renamed, or retyped, a required field added to a request, a status code's meaning changed. A client written against the previous version breaks.
  • MINOR — an addition. A new route, a new optional request field, a new response field, a new value of an enumerated response field. A client written against the previous version keeps working unmodified.
  • PATCH — a clarification of the document that changes no shape.

A new value of an enumerated response field is a MINOR change because the protocol requires a client to accept a value it does not recognize. The reader rules state that requirement for every response enum that can grow: a deck entry's model category, and a problem document's domain, retry and next_step.kind, a suggested fix's safety and its operations' kind (Readers and emitters), and a run's status, which can grow only by a status of a run that has not ended. The validate report's true and false verdict flags cannot grow, and a response enum the protocol adds later states a reader rule of its own. A client written to the rules keeps working. A client that rejected unknown values breaks all the same, so the changelog marks such a change breaking, the way it marks a minor standard change that a runtime has to follow.

A problem's code is not an enumerated field. The protocol fixes a code's shape and leaves which codes exist to the registries, so a new code, in the core registry or under a registered prefix, moves no protocol number; a reader that does not know it reads it by its family. A change to the core registry moves the standard version instead.

A recommended extension field is none of those additions. What the protocol version numbers is the base surface — the routes and the response fields of the normative OpenAPI document. The artifacts the standard names on the validate report's extension surface are shaped by their own specification pages and ride a report that is extension-open by policy, so naming one moves no protocol number: a runner may report or omit any of them at the same protocol version, and a client learns which it got from the report itself rather than from the handshake.

The shape of a stuff — the {concept, content} entries of a request's inputs and of pipe_output — is the standard's for the same reason: the protocol names the fields and the CLI I/O contract fixes their entries, so a change to that shape moves the standard version and leaves the protocol number where it was.

The problem document crosses the same boundary the other way. It is the protocol's, and the CLI I/O contract has a CLI write it on stderr, without its status member, when a method fails. A CLI implementing a standard version writes the problem document of the protocol version that the same release names on its changelog heading, and a reader learns which protocol version that is from the standard version the CLI implements. A release that changes the problem document therefore changes what a CLI writes as well, and its standard version moves by the rules above for a change to what a runtime emits.

The protocol version is not derived from the standard version and never tracks it. A release of the standard that does not touch the protocol leaves the protocol version exactly where it was.

docs.title: The Changelog Contract
docs.text:
Every released version heading in CHANGELOG.md names the two versions it carries:

## [v2.1.0] - 2026-10-14

**MTHDS standard 2.1.0 · MTHDS Protocol 0.6.0**

The standard version always equals the heading's own version, by the rule above. The protocol version is repeated on every heading whether or not it moved, so that a reader landing on any release can tell which protocol it shipped without walking backwards through the file.

While a release is being prepared, the entries accumulate under a single ## [Unreleased] heading that announces the version it will cut, in the same form.

docs.title: Where the Numbers Appear
docs.text:
Number Where Standard The specification's release version and its changelog headings Standard MTHDS_STANDARD_VERSION in each implementation Standard The version native-concepts.md pins its set at (the last version in which the set changed) Standard A manifest's mthds_version constraint, evaluated against the runtime's standard version Standard A library crate's mthds_version stamp Standard The version of the core error registry and of its snapshot Protocol info.version in mthds-protocol.openapi.yaml Protocol protocol_version in every GET /version response Protocol The conformance statement in the protocol specification

An implementation's copies of these numbers are exactly that — copies of a cut made here. Each SHOULD be declared once, in one place, naming this page as its source, so that following a cut is a single edit rather than a search.

docs.title: History: The 2.0.0 Unification
docs.text:
The numbers above were not always one system. Before 2.0.0, the specification published its own release numbers, from v0.0.1 up to v0.10.0, while MTHDS_STANDARD_VERSION sat at 1.0.0 — set alongside v0.1.0 in February 2026 and never moved after that, through the removal of a native concept, the addition of another, three natives whose shape changed, and a set of breaking manifest, lock and resolution rules. Manifests constrained >=1.0.0, crates were stamped 1.0.0, and neither number said what the standard had actually become.

2.0.0 is the cut that pays that debt and unifies the two numbers into one:

  • It is a major bump because the changes it accounts for are breaking — see the changelog entries for v0.8.0, v0.9.0, and v0.10.0.
  • It moves forwards from 1.0.0, so no manifest in the wild is invalidated by the unification itself: a constraint of >=1.0.0 remains satisfiable against 2.0.0.
  • Crate stamps are the one thing it does not carry over, and they cannot be: 2.0.0 is the first version at which a native set is pinned, so the resolution rule above has nothing to resolve a stamp below it to. A crate stamped 1.0.0 predates the pinning regime — its materialized natives came from whatever its producer happened to hold, which is precisely the debt this cut pays. Re-normalizing such a crate against a conforming implementation materializes the set pinned at 2.0.0 and restamps it.
  • From 2.0.0 onward there is one standard version, and it moves on every release of this specification under the rules above.

The protocol number was reconciled at the same time and kept its value. 0.6.0 is what the normative OpenAPI document and the shipped client libraries had been reporting; the readings that disagreed — a 0.1.0 in a hosted implementation and a "v0.1" in this specification's own conformance sentence — were corrected to follow it.

docs.title: Editor Support
docs.text: The Pipelex extension for VS Code-compatible editors (VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity, and others) provides syntax highlighting, semantic tokens, formatting, and validation for .mthds files. It is also available on Open VSX. It is the recommended way to work with MTHDS.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the Pipelex extension from the VS Code Marketplace:

  1. Open your VS Code-compatible editor.
  2. Go to Extensions (Ctrl+Shift+X / Cmd+Shift+X).
  3. Search for Pipelex.
  4. Click Install.

The extension activates automatically for .mthds files.

docs.title: Syntax Highlighting
docs.text:
The extension provides a full TextMate grammar for .mthds files, built on top of TOML highlighting. It recognizes MTHDS-specific constructs: pipe sections, concept sections, prompt templates, Jinja2 variables ({{ }}, @variable, $variable), and HTML content embedded in prompts.

Markdown code blocks tagged as mthds or toml also receive syntax highlighting when the extension is active.

docs.title: Semantic Tokens
docs.text:
Beyond TextMate grammar-based highlighting, the extension provides 7 semantic token types that distinguish MTHDS-specific elements:

Token type Applies to Visual hint mthdsConcept Concept names (e.g., ContractClause, Text) Type color mthdsPipeType Pipe type values (e.g., PipeLLM, PipeSequence) Type color, bold mthdsDataVariable Data variables in prompts Variable color mthdsPipeName Pipe names in references Function color mthdsPipeSection Pipe section headers ([pipe.my_pipe]) Keyword color, bold mthdsConceptSection Concept section headers ([concept.MyConcept]) Keyword color, bold mthdsModelRef Model field references ($preset, @alias) Variable color, bold

Semantic tokens are enabled by default. To toggle them:

  • pipelex.mthds.semanticTokens — MTHDS-specific semantic tokens.
  • pipelex.syntax.semanticTokens — TOML table/array key tokens.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
The extension includes a built-in formatter for .mthds and .toml files. It uses the same engine as the plxt CLI (see Formatting & Linting). Format on save works out of the box.

Formatting options are configurable in VS Code settings under pipelex.formatter.* (e.g., alignEntries, columnWidth, trailingNewline).

docs.title: Schema Validation
docs.text:
The extension supports JSON Schema-based validation and completion for TOML files. When the MTHDS JSON Schema is configured (see MTHDS JSON Schema), the editor provides:

  • Autocomplete suggestions for field names and values.
  • Inline validation errors for invalid fields or types.
  • Hover documentation for known fields.

Schema support is enabled by default (pipelex.schema.enabled).

docs.title: Additional Commands
docs.text:
The extension contributes several commands accessible via the Command Palette:

Command Description TOML: Copy as JSON Copy selected TOML as JSON. TOML: Copy as TOML Copy selected text as TOML. TOML: Paste as JSON Paste clipboard content as JSON. TOML: Paste as TOML Paste clipboard content as TOML. TOML: Select Schema Choose a JSON Schema for the current TOML file. Copy Markdown

docs.title: Formatting & Linting
docs.text: plxt is the CLI tool for formatting and linting .mthds and .toml files. It ensures consistent style across MTHDS projects.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: plxt is distributed as a standalone binary. Install it from the pipelex-tools PyPI package (uv tool install pipelex-tools), or use the bundled version included with the VS Code extension.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
Format .mthds and .toml files in place:

# Format all .mthds and .toml files in the current directory (recursive)
plxt format .

# Format a single file
plxt format contract_analysis.mthds

# Format and see what changed (check mode — exits non-zero if changes needed)
plxt format --check .

The plxt format command (also available as plxt fmt) aligns entries, normalizes whitespace, and ensures consistent TOML style. Files are modified in place.

docs.title: Linting
docs.text:
Lint .mthds and .toml files for structural issues:

# Lint all files in the current directory
plxt lint .

# Lint a single file
plxt lint contract_analysis.mthds

The plxt lint command checks for TOML structural issues and reports errors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
plxt reads its configuration from a .pipelex/plxt.toml file in the project root or a parent directory. This file controls formatting rules (alignment, column width, trailing commas, etc.) and can define per-file-type overrides.

A basic configuration:

[formatting]
align_entries      = true
column_width       = 100
trailing_newline   = true
array_trailing_comma = true

For the full list of configuration options, see the Pipelex documentation.

docs.title: Editor Integration
docs.text:
When the VS Code extension is installed, plxt formatting runs automatically on save. The extension uses the same formatting engine, so files formatted via CLI and editor produce identical results.
